title: Tenant Who Stays After the Lease Ends
bodyText:
If a tenant stays after a fixed-term lease ends, the holding over is not by itself evidence that you agreed to a new lease, and an oral lease at a monthly rent with no agreed end is a lease for one month only.

To remove the tenant you must serve a notice to quit through a proper officer and bring a summary process case in court (unless a valid lease waiver of the notice to quit applies).

While the case is pending, the court can order the tenant to pay use and occupancy into court equal to the last agreed rent, or the fair rental value if there was no agreed rent.

If you accept money after the date to quit, you can reserve your rights by including the statutory use-and-occupancy disclaimer in the notice to quit; accepting rent you know is overdue waives the right to end the tenancy for that late rent.

A tenant in a building or complex of five or more units (or a mobile home park) who is 62 or older or has a disability expected to last at least 12 months or to result in death, or who permanently lives with a spouse, sibling, parent or grandparent who is 62 or older or a spouse, sibling, child, parent or grandparent with such a disability, cannot be evicted just because the lease ended; in a condominium or other common interest community this applies only to conversion tenants or where you own five or more units in that community.

title: No Premium Holdover Charge Offered
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute that sets or caps a holdover charge, so a lease could try to set a daily or premium rate for a tenant who stays after the lease ends. We do not offer one. For most of a holdover the statutes already set the measure: while an eviction case is pending the court, on your motion, orders use and occupancy payments at the last agreed rent (or at fair rental value if the tenant objects), and during a court-granted stay of execution the court may require payments at the rent the tenant was paying or another reasonable amount. A premium charge could also fall on a tenant who has a legal right to stay, such as a protected tenant 62 or older or with a disability, and an unreasonable fixed charge may be an unenforceable penalty. If you want a holdover charge anyway, have your own lawyer draft it.

title: Pet Fees and Pet Deposits
bodyText: You may not charge a pet fee, or any fee other than the first month's rent, a security deposit, a key or special-equipment deposit and the capped screening-report fee, before or at the start of a tenancy. Connecticut law does not clearly say whether a pet deposit may be taken as a separate charge, so collect any pet deposit only as part of the security deposit: it counts toward the two-month limit (one month for a tenant 62 or older), must be held in escrow and earns interest. Monthly pet rent is ordinary rent and is allowed. If you advertise the unit, you may leave a pet fee or pet deposit out of the advertised rent. You may not charge any pet fee or deposit for an assistance animal.

title: Last Month's Rent Counts as a Deposit
bodyText: In Connecticut any rent paid in advance, other than the first month's rent, is a security deposit. Last month's rent collected at signing therefore counts toward the deposit limit of two months' rent (one month for a tenant 62 or older), must be deposited in an escrow account at a Connecticut financial institution, must be reported to the tenant with the bank's name and address within 30 days, and earns interest at the Banking Commissioner's deposit index. It is returned or applied under the security deposit rules when the tenancy ends.

title: How Tenants May Pay Rent
bodyText:
You may not require electronic payment (an online portal, ACH or autopay) as the only way to pay rent or the security deposit; always accept at least one paper method such as a check or money order.

Connecticut's surcharge law also bars adding a fee because a person pays by a particular method, and it covers renting real property.

The rent-advertising law mentions payment-processing fees, but Connecticut's statutes don't settle whether that allows one on rent, so the safe course is not to add a card or portal convenience fee to rent. If you charge one anyway after legal advice, it must reflect your actual cost and you must offer a fee-free way to pay, or the fee must be built into the advertised rent.

Give a written receipt for every cash payment.

title: Rent-Pricing Software Banned
bodyText: Since January 1, 2026, you may not use revenue management software to set rents or occupancy levels for Connecticut homes. The ban covers any software or device that runs calculations on nonpublic competitor data, such as other landlords' actual rents, occupancy or lease dates, to advise you whether to leave a unit vacant or how much rent to charge. Published reports of aggregated rental data that do not recommend rents, and tools used to set rent or income limits under an affordable housing program, are not covered. A violation is enforced under Connecticut's antitrust law.

title: Application and Screening Fees
bodyText: You may not charge an application or processing fee. The only charge you may take from an applicant is a fee for a tenant screening report (credit, criminal background, employment or rental history), and it may not exceed $50 plus the yearly inflation adjustment the Connecticut Department of Housing sets. If you charge it, give the applicant a copy of the report (or, if you may not share it, the information needed to request it from the screening company) and a copy of the screening company's receipt or invoice. These limits also bind a property manager, screening company or other third party acting for you. You may never charge a move-in or move-out fee.

title: Advertised Rent Must Include Recurring Fees
bodyText: When you advertise, display or offer a unit, the rent you state must include every fee or cost the tenant will have to pay on a periodic basis, prorated into the rent figure. A fee charged monthly by default counts even if the tenant can opt out of it. You may leave out only: a payment-processing fee that reflects actual cost when you offer a fee-free way to pay; a pet fee or deposit; utilities that are submetered or paid directly to a utility and vary month to month; a charge for damage beyond normal wear and tear; and a separate fee for a service such as a lockout or key replacement. A violation makes you liable to the tenant for one month's rent, plus possible attorney's fees. The same total periodic rent goes on the state's Rental Terms Summary Form that must be the first page of the lease.

title: No Specific Rule on Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute that specifically bars charging a fee for a service you do not provide. Several related rules do apply. You may not charge a heat or utilities surcharge when heat or utilities are included in the rent, and for leases signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, you may not charge the tenant for utilities that are not measured by a separate meter serving only the tenant's unit. You may not charge a move-in or move-out fee. Make sure every fee in your lease pays for something real.

title: Which Charges Count as Rent
bodyText: Connecticut defines rent as all periodic payments the lease requires the tenant to make to you. A recurring charge such as monthly pet rent or a monthly parking fee is therefore rent, which means it counts for the 45-day rent-increase notice. A required periodic fee must also be built into your advertised rent and the total rent on the state's Rental Terms Summary Form, except the fees the advertising law lets you leave out, such as a pet fee or deposit, submetered or directly paid utilities, and fees for a service you perform for the tenant. One-time charges, such as a late charge, a returned-payment charge or a repair bill, are not periodic and so are not rent; calling them "additional rent" in the lease is not supported by any statute. Connecticut's statutes don't say whether that label would let you evict for an unpaid one-time charge, so don't base a nonpayment notice to quit on one. Never base a nonpayment notice to quit on an unpaid lock-change cost or an unpaid bed bug assistance repayment; the law forbids it.

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: No Connecticut statute addresses making a tenant reimburse you for a fee a town or other government charges you, such as a rental registration or inspection fee. The library does not offer such a clause. In Connecticut any recurring payment the lease requires is rent, every recurring fee (other than a few listed exceptions, such as a pet fee or separately metered utilities, none of which covers a government fee) must be built into the rent you advertise and into the total rent on the state's Rental Terms Summary Form, and a violation costs one month's rent; a fee whose amount you don't know when you sign can't meet those rules. If you want to recover a government fee, build it into the rent, or get legal advice before adding your own clause. Check your town's rental licensing or registration rules separately.

title: Late Charge Limits and Grace Period
bodyText: You may charge a late charge only if the written lease provides for one, and only after the grace period ends: nine days after rent is due, or four days in a week-to-week tenancy, plus five more days for any month or week when your online payment system kept the tenant from paying. The charge may not exceed the lesser of $5 a day up to $50, or 5% of the late rent payment (5% of the tenant's share if a government agency or charity pays part of the rent). You may charge only one late charge per late payment, however long it stays unpaid, and you may not offer a discount for paying within the grace period. A lease term that charges earlier or more is unenforceable. If you knowingly accept overdue rent, you give up the right to end the tenancy for that late payment.

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule
bodyText: Connecticut has no rule requiring the same rent or terms for a month-to-month tenancy and a fixed-term lease, and no cap on the rent difference between them. Unless the lease fixes a definite term, the tenancy is month to month (week to week if rent is paid weekly). Whatever the lease type, a rent increase needs written notice at least 45 days before it takes effect (for a tenancy with a term of one month or less, notice equal to one full term), and the notice rule does not let you raise rent during a fixed term unless the lease allows it.

title: No Rule on Notice Fees
bodyText: No Connecticut statute addresses charging a tenant for preparing or serving a notice, such as a notice to quit. In Connecticut a notice to quit must be served by a proper officer, such as a state marshal, and if you win a summary process (eviction) case the judgment includes your court costs. The library offers an optional clause that lets you recover only your actual cost of having a notice served, and not a second time as court costs. Any attorney's fee a lease makes the tenant pay is capped at 15% of a money judgment.

title: Rent Concessions
bodyText: No Connecticut statute regulates rent concessions such as a free month or a move-in discount. If you give one, state it in the lease with its amount and the rental periods it covers. Do not offer a discount for paying rent early or on time: a lease may not let a tenant pay a reduced rent for paying within the statutory grace period (nine days for monthly rent). A clause that makes the tenant repay a concession after a default may be treated by a court as a penalty, so the library does not offer one.

title: No Rent Control, but Fair Rent Commissions
bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide limit on how much you can raise rent. But every town or city with 15,000 or more people must have, or join, a fair rent commission by January 1, 2028, and smaller towns may have one. A tenant (other than in a seasonal rental of 120 days or less a year) can complain to the commission about rent, a proposed increase, or any fee you charge, and the commission can limit it if it finds it harsh and unconscionable, or suspend rent until you fix code violations. Ignoring a commission order can bring fines for each day. For protected tenants (62 or older or with a disability expected to last at least 12 months or to result in death, or permanently living with a spouse, sibling, parent or grandparent who is 62 or older or a spouse, sibling, child, parent or grandparent with such a disability, in a building or complex of five or more units or a mobile home park; in a condominium or other common interest community only for conversion tenants or where you own five or more units there), increases must be fair and equitable under the same factors. Check your town's commission and ordinance.

title: Rent Increase Notice
bodyText:
No rent increase takes effect unless you give the tenant written notice at least 45 days before it starts; for a tenancy of one month or less, give notice equal to one full rental period. A tenant who does not answer has not agreed to the increase. The notice rule does not let you raise rent during a fixed term unless the lease allows it.

You may not demand a rent increase within six months after a tenant in good faith complains to officials or a fair rent commission, asks for repairs, sues to enforce repairs, or organizes or joins a tenants' union, or after a town agency or official files a notice, complaint or order about a code violation, unless the problem was caused by the tenant's household or guests, or you became liable for a substantial increase in taxes or operating costs (not tied to fixing the complaint) at least four months before the demand and the increase does not exceed your prorated share of that net increase.

In a building or complex of five or more units or a mobile home park, a tenant who is 62 or older or has a disability expected to last at least 12 months or to result in death, or who permanently lives with a spouse, sibling, parent or grandparent who is 62 or older or a spouse, sibling, child, parent or grandparent with such a disability, may get only fair and equitable increases (in a condominium or other common interest community, only conversion tenants or where you own five or more units there).

title: Raising Rent During the Term
bodyText:
Connecticut law does not itself let you raise rent during a fixed term; any increase during the term must come from the lease. The library's optional clause lets you list scheduled increases in the lease.

Connecticut's statutes don't say whether a lease may instead let you raise rent at will during the term, and a tenant's failure to respond to an increase notice is not agreement to it, so the library does not offer an open-ended increase clause.

You must give written notice at least 45 days before each increase, even one listed in the lease.

An increase can still be challenged before a local fair rent commission, must be fair and equitable for a tenant in a building or complex of five or more units or a mobile home park who is 62 or older or has a disability expected to last at least 12 months or to result in death, or who permanently lives with a spouse, sibling, parent or grandparent who is 62 or older or a spouse, sibling, child, parent or grandparent with such a disability (in a condominium or other common interest community, only conversion tenants or where you own five or more units there), and may not be retaliatory.

title: Cash Receipts and Rent Ledger
bodyText: Whenever you receive a cash payment from or for an occupant, give the person who paid a receipt showing the date, the amount and what the payment was for. If an occupant asks, you must also give them a copy of the ledger or other accounting for their unit, showing the charges, the payments and any balance owed or overpaid. Keep your records in a form you can produce on request.

title: No Rent Reporting Rule
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring you to offer tenants positive rent reporting to credit bureaus, and none regulating whether you report rent payments or require a tenant to join a rent-reporting program. If you report payment data, federal credit reporting law applies. Any program fee charged before or at the start of the tenancy would run into Connecticut's ban on up-front fees other than a deposit, first month's rent, a key deposit and a screening-report fee.

title: Sales Tax and Short Stays
bodyText: Connecticut does not charge sales tax on ordinary residential rent. Its room occupancy tax applies to stays of 30 consecutive days or less in a hotel, a bed and breakfast, or a lodging house, which includes a furnished residence or similar accommodation. The rate is 15% of the rent (11% for a bed and breakfast) for the first 30 days. If you rent a furnished home for short stays, you may owe this tax; a short-term rental platform may collect it for you, and your town may require a short-term rental license.

title: Put Every Fee in the Lease
bodyText: No Connecticut statute requires your lease to list every fee or bars a fee the lease does not mention. Several rules make listing them the only safe course. A late charge is allowed only under a written agreement in the lease. Every recurring fee, apart from a few listed exceptions such as pet fees and separately metered utilities, must be built into the advertised rent and the total rent on the state's Rental Terms Summary Form. Up-front charges are limited to a security deposit, first month's rent, a key or equipment deposit and a capped screening-report fee. A rule you adopt after signing that substantially changes the lease, such as a new fee, is not valid unless the tenant agrees in writing.

title: No Government Shutdown Protection
bodyText: No Connecticut statute gives tenants who are government workers extra time to pay rent, or a defense to eviction, during a federal or state government shutdown. The usual nine-day grace period, late-charge limits and eviction rules apply. Agreeing to a written payment plan can avoid a costly eviction case.

title: Connecticut's Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: Connecticut sets these limits, whatever the lease says. Security deposit: no more than two months' rent, or one month's rent for a tenant 62 or older. Late charge: only after the grace period (nine days, four for a weekly tenancy, plus five more days when your online payment system kept the tenant from paying), no more than the lesser of $5 a day up to $50 or 5% of the late payment, and only once per late payment. Screening-report fee: $50 plus the state's yearly inflation adjustment; no other application fee, and no move-in or move-out fee. Bounced check: up to $20. Attorney's fees the lease makes the tenant pay: no more than 15% of a money judgment. Changing locks for a tenant protected by a court order: actual reasonable cost only.

title: Late Charges When a Subsidy Pays Part of the Rent
bodyText: If a government agency or charity pays part of the rent, any late charge is capped at 5% of the tenant's own share of the late payment (or $5 a day up to $50, if less). Connecticut law does not say whether you may charge the tenant a late charge when the tenant paid their share on time and only the agency's payment was late; the safe course is not to. Housing program rules (for example, a Housing Choice Voucher contract) may also limit late charges.

title: Passing On Property Tax Increases
bodyText: No Connecticut statute addresses a lease clause that passes real estate tax increases on to a tenant, and the library does not offer one. Any rent increase needs 45 days' written notice (one full term for a tenancy of one month or less), and during a fixed term rent can change only as the lease allows (see the optional Rent Changes During the Term clause). Within six months after a tenant's protected complaint you may raise rent only by your prorated share of a substantial tax or operating-cost increase (not tied to fixing the complaint) that you became liable for at least four months before the demand, or where the tenant's household or guests caused the problem.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText:
Do not charge interest on late rent. Connecticut allows only one late charge per late rent payment, and a lease may not require more; the statutes don't say whether interest on late rent counts as a second late charge, so the safe course is not to charge it.

For other money a tenant owes, such as repair costs beyond the security deposit, Connecticut's legal interest rate is 8% a year unless the lease sets a different rate, and in a lawsuit a court may award interest of no more than 10% a year for money held back after it was due. The library offers an optional clause setting interest on unpaid non-rent amounts.

title: Renting to Veterans
bodyText: No Connecticut program pays landlords an incentive or tax credit for renting to veterans. Connecticut's Department of Housing must give eligible veterans priority in its security deposit guarantee program, under which the state guarantees payment for tenant damage, up to two months' rent, instead of the tenant paying a cash deposit. Status as a veteran is protected under Connecticut's fair housing law, so you may not refuse to rent to, or treat differently, an applicant because they are a veteran. That law does not apply when you rent a room in a single-family home you live in, or a unit in a two-family building where you live in the other unit.

title: Accepting Late Rent Waives Termination
bodyText: If you accept rent knowing it is overdue, you give up the right to end the tenancy for not paying that rent on time, and a lease clause saying otherwise does not change that. If you have served a notice to quit and want to keep the eviction going, you may include in the notice the statement Connecticut law provides: "Any payments tendered after the date specified to quit possession or occupancy, or the date of the completion of the pretermination process if that is later, will be accepted for use and occupancy only and not for rent, with full reservation of rights to continue with the eviction action." The statement takes effect only after the quit date. Connecticut's statutes don't say what happens if you accept money after the quit date without the statement, or whether a partial payment counts as accepting rent, so get legal advice before accepting any money during an eviction.

title: Move-In Walk-Through
bodyText: For a lease entered into on or after January 1, 2024, after the lease is signed but before the tenant moves in, you must offer the tenant a joint walk-through of the unit. If the tenant accepts, you both must use the Department of Housing's preoccupancy walk-through checklist, note every existing condition, defect or damage, and each sign and keep a copy. You may not keep any part of the security deposit, or ask the tenant to pay, for anything noted on the checklist. The checklist can be used as evidence but is not conclusive. Connecticut does not require a move-out inspection, but doing one and keeping photos helps if deductions are disputed.

title: No Preset Deposit Charges
bodyText: Do not put a schedule of fixed cleaning, carpet or repair charges in the lease to take from the security deposit. Connecticut lets you keep only the value of damages you actually suffer because the tenant did not meet the tenant's obligations: unpaid rent or utility payments owed to you, damage or uncleanliness that breaches the tenant's legal duties, and an unpaid lock-change cost. Every deduction must be listed in an itemized written statement. You may never deduct for a condition noted on the move-in walk-through checklist, or for normal wear.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds
bodyText: A deposit refund your former tenant never receives or never cashes does not become yours. Under Connecticut's unclaimed property law, money you owe someone that stays unclaimed for more than three years after it became payable is presumed abandoned. In that year, between July 1 and September 30, you must try to reach the tenant by first-class mail (if the total is $50 or more) and by email if they agreed to email notices; if they still don't claim it, you must report it and pay it to the State Treasurer by the next March 31. You may not charge a dormancy or similar fee, and the lease may not say the deposit is forfeited if unclaimed.

title: Paying the Deposit in Installments
bodyText: Connecticut gives most tenants no right to pay the security deposit in installments, so you may require it in full before move-in. You may agree to installments; if you do, put the schedule in writing, and remember every installment is part of the deposit and must go into the escrow account. Housing authorities and other state-assisted providers of public housing for older adults and people with disabilities must allow installments over at least twelve months.

title: No Conditions on the Deposit Refund
bodyText: You may not make the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving you advance notice of moving out. Return the deposit, with interest and any itemized deductions, within 21 days after the tenancy ends, or within 15 days after you receive the tenant's written forwarding address, whichever is later. A lease term that adds conditions to the refund is unenforceable, and a late or missing return can make you liable for twice the deposit.

title: Deposit After a Violence-Based Termination
bodyText: Connecticut has no special deposit rule when a tenant ends a lease early because of family violence or sexual assault; the normal deposit return rules apply. You may still deduct unpaid rent owed before the termination date and the cost of damage the tenant caused. If other tenants on the lease stay, they remain bound by it, and the law does not say how to split the deposit between the departing and remaining tenants; get advice before returning any part of it.

title: Returning the Deposit Early
bodyText: Connecticut has no special early-return procedure for security deposits. You may return all or part of a deposit sooner than the law requires, even during the tenancy, but you must then pay the interest that has built up on the amount returned within 21 days. You may not deduct an administrative or processing fee; only damages from the tenant's failure to meet the tenant's obligations may be kept.

title: Fees Instead of a Deposit
bodyText: No Connecticut landlord-tenant statute authorizes a fee or insurance product that a tenant pays instead of a security deposit, and the library does not offer one. You may not charge any fee at or before move-in other than a security deposit, the first month's rent, a key or equipment deposit and a capped screening-report fee. A monthly fee in place of a deposit would be rent: it must be built into your advertised rent and the total rent on the state's Rental Terms Summary Form. You may accept a state security deposit guarantee from the Department of Housing in place of a cash deposit for eligible tenants; to be paid for damage, you must file a claim with repair receipts within 20 days after the tenancy ends.

title: No Holding Fees
bodyText: Connecticut does not allow a separate fee or deposit just to hold a unit. Before or at the start of a tenancy you may collect only a security deposit, the first month's rent, a key or special-equipment deposit, and a capped screening-report fee, and the same limit applies to a property manager or anyone acting for you. If you take money to hold a unit, treat it as the security deposit or the first month's rent: a security deposit must go into an escrow account, counts toward the deposit limit and earns interest. The law does not say you may keep that money if the applicant decides not to rent, so get advice before keeping any of it.

title: No Nonrefundable Deposits or Move-In Fees
bodyText: Connecticut has no such thing as a nonrefundable deposit. Any money you collect in advance, other than the first month's rent or a deposit for a key or special equipment, is a security deposit: it stays the tenant's property, goes into escrow, earns interest, counts toward the deposit limit, and may be kept only for actual damages from the tenant's breach. You may not charge a nonrefundable cleaning, pet, administrative or move-in fee at or before the start of the tenancy, and you may never charge a move-in or move-out fee.

title: Security Deposit Limit
bodyText: You may not ask for a security deposit of more than two months' rent, or more than one month's rent if the tenant is 62 or older. If a tenant turns 62 after paying a larger deposit, you must return the part above one month's rent when the tenant asks. Every advance payment except the first month's rent and a key or special-equipment deposit, including last month's rent and any pet deposit, counts toward the limit. The Banking Department enforces the limit and, starting October 1, 2026, can order civil penalties.

title: No Penalty Tied to the Walk-Through Offer
bodyText: Connecticut requires you to offer a move-in walk-through but sets no specific penalty, such as losing the right to make deposit deductions, for failing to offer it, and it has no move-out inspection notice rule. Skipping the offer still breaks the law and leaves you without the signed checklist, which is often your best evidence of the unit's condition at move-in. Always make and document the offer.

title: Escrow Account for Deposits
bodyText:
Put the whole security deposit into an escrow account for the tenant at a bank, savings bank or savings and loan association located in Connecticut (a credit union does not qualify) as soon as you receive it; the account must be one your creditors cannot reach.

Within 30 days after you receive the deposit, or move it to another institution or account, give the tenant written notice of the amount held and the name and address of the institution.

Take money out only to return it, pay interest, move it to a new owner or account, keep excess interest, or keep amounts for proven damages after the tenancy ends. If the Banking Department asks about a deposit, answer within 7 days.

Knowingly mishandling deposits can bring a fine of up to $500 and up to 30 days in jail per offense, unless you rented to fewer than four deposit-paying tenants.

title: Interest on Security Deposits
bodyText: You must pay interest on every security deposit at no less than the rate the Banking Commissioner sets for each calendar year (the deposit index; 0.49% for 2026). On each anniversary of the tenancy, pay the interest to the tenant or credit it to the next rent. When the tenancy ends, or if you return any part of the deposit early, pay the interest that has built up within 21 days. You may skip interest only for a month in which rent was more than ten days late and you did not charge a late charge. You may not raise rent because you must pay interest, and a lease cannot make the tenant give up interest. Housing owned by a school for its students is exempt.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A lease cannot make a tenant give up any right under Connecticut's security deposit law, including the right to interest on the deposit. A lease term that tries to do so is unenforceable. Also note that Connecticut deposit rules apply whatever the lease calls the payment: any advance payment other than the first month's rent or a key or special-equipment deposit is a security deposit.

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: When you sell or otherwise transfer a rented property, you must take the tenants' deposits, plus the interest they have earned, out of escrow and deliver them to the new owner. The new owner takes over your rights in the deposits and must return them when each tenancy ends, even though you collected them. Give the tenant written notice of the sale: unless agreed otherwise, a seller to a good-faith buyer is released from the lease and landlord-tenant duties only for events after that notice. The new owner must give the tenant a new escrow notice within 30 days and its own name and address for notices.

title: Penalties for Late or Missing Deposit Returns
bodyText: If you miss the deposit deadline (21 days after the tenancy ends, or 15 days after you get the tenant's written forwarding address, whichever is later), or fail to send the itemized statement of deductions, you can owe the tenant twice the full deposit. If the only problem is that you left out the interest, you owe $10 or twice the interest, whichever is more. Knowingly and wilfully failing to return a deposit when due can also bring a fine of up to $250, unless you honestly believed you were entitled to deduct for damages. The tenant can sue to get the deposit back, and the Banking Department can investigate complaints and, from October 1, 2026, order civil penalties, but it does not decide good-faith disputes over damages you itemized.

title: No Deposit Standards Disclosure
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to post or disclose the standards you use to set deposit amounts. Every deposit is still capped at two months' rent, or one month's rent for a tenant 62 or older, and fair housing law bars setting different deposit terms because of a protected characteristic such as race, familial status, lawful source of income or status as a veteran. Using written, uniform criteria is the safest practice.

title: No Separate Utility Deposit
bodyText: Connecticut has no separate utility deposit for landlords. If you collect money in advance to cover utility bills the tenant owes you, it is part of the security deposit: it counts toward the two-month (or one-month for 62+) limit, goes into escrow, earns interest and must be returned under the normal deposit rules. Unpaid utility charges owed to you can already be deducted from the security deposit at the end of the tenancy.

title: Alterations Tenants May Make Without Your Consent
bodyText: Your lease may require your consent before a tenant alters the unit, but Connecticut gives tenants some rights you cannot take away. A tenant may install energy conservation measures at no cost to you after sending you written notice by certified mail; the work may go ahead unless you send a written disapproval by certified mail within 20 days, and you can never block removable weatherstripping, removable interior storm windows or insulation wrap on the water heater. You must allow reasonable modifications a tenant with a disability needs, at the tenant's expense, and you may, where reasonable, require the tenant to restore the interior when they leave. A tenant with a dedicated parking space may ask to install an EV charging station under separate rules.

title: Bed Bug Duties
bodyText:
These rules apply to every rental unit except a single-family detached home.

When a tenant reports bed bugs, you must inspect, or have a qualified inspector inspect, the unit and any connected unit you own within five business days, and if you inspect yourself, give the tenant written results within two days with local health department contact information.

If bed bugs are found, begin effective treatment within five business days; if you treat without a pest control agent, vacuum first and get a qualified re-inspection within five business days.

You pay for inspection and treatment; the tenant pays to prepare the unit, must allow access on reasonable notice, and is liable for extra treatments caused by knowingly and unreasonably refusing to cooperate.

Offer reasonable help to a tenant who physically cannot prepare; you may charge a reasonable amount on a repayment plan of up to six months, but missed payments are not grounds for eviction (you may deduct the balance from the deposit at move-out).

Failing these duties can cost you the tenant's attorney's fees and at least $250; if a tenant refuses access or cooperation, you may ask the court for an order.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacate Notice Rule
bodyText: Connecticut has no rule requiring a tenant to tell you before leaving the unit empty in cold weather. Connecticut does require a tenant, unless the lease says otherwise, to tell you about any anticipated extended absence, and you may then enter at reasonable times to inspect or make repairs. The library's extended-absence clause covers this; it helps you protect pipes and heating while the unit is empty.

title: Common-Area Lighting
bodyText: In a building with three or more households sharing halls or stairways, you must light all public halls at night, and in every building you must keep common areas clean and safe. Do not put hallway, stairway or other common-area lights on a tenant's electric meter. For leases signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, a lease term making a tenant pay for utilities billed to the tenant without a separate meter that measures only what is delivered to that tenant's unit is unenforceable, and Connecticut's utility law makes you responsible for electricity supplied to the building except service metered for one unit's exclusive use. The statutes don't say exactly how these rules apply to a tenant's own account that also carries common lights, so if common lights are on a tenant's meter now, plan to rewire them or put that service in your name.

title: Liens for Work a Tenant Orders
bodyText: In Connecticut, a contractor who works on the property under a contract with your tenant can put a mechanic's lien on the tenant's leasehold. If the work was done with your consent, the contractor may also claim a lien on your building and land. Connecticut's statutes don't say whether approving a tenant's alteration counts as that consent, so treat any approval as possibly exposing your property to a lien. No Connecticut statute lets a lease clause block that. Before approving any tenant alteration, decide whether you want to allow it at all, require the tenant to show that contractors have been paid, and get advice on lien waivers for larger jobs.

title: Family Child Care in Rentals
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to let a tenant run a family child care home in your rental, and sets no lease conditions for one. Towns may not use zoning to treat a licensed family child care home differently from any other home, and the tenant must hold a license from the Office of Early Childhood. Because the library's lease limits the unit to residential use, a tenant needs your written consent to run a child care business; if you consent, consider requiring proof of the license and of liability insurance.

title: No Home Business Right
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute giving tenants a right to run a business from a rental home, so the lease decides. By law a tenant must use the unit only as a home unless you agree otherwise, and the library's lease limits use to residential purposes. If you want to allow quiet work from home or a small business, say so in writing; local zoning rules on home occupations still apply.

title: Water and Sewer Liens on Rental Property
bodyText: In Connecticut, unpaid municipal water and sewer charges become a lien on the property they served and a charge against the owner, collected like unpaid property taxes, even if a tenant ran up the bill. No lease clause or filing protects you from that. A private water company can lien the property only if the owner of record is the one who owes the charges. If tenants pay water or sewer directly, check the account status regularly; and in a lease signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, a lease term making a tenant pay for utilities billed to the tenant without a separate meter serving only that unit is unenforceable.

title: Occupancy Limits
bodyText:
Connecticut has no statewide limit on people per bedroom for private rentals.

In a building with three or more households, or a lodging or boarding house, the local health department can order a room's occupants reduced so that each person over 12 has at least 500 cubic feet of air and each child under 12 at least 300 cubic feet. The State Building Code and local housing codes may set other limits.

Fair housing law protects families with children and expressly preserves only reasonable state and local occupancy limits. Whether a stricter limit you set yourself is lawful isn't settled by the statutes, so don't set a limit stricter than the codes that apply to your property.

title: Smoking, Vaping and Cannabis
bodyText:
You may ban smoking and vaping of tobacco and cannabis anywhere on the property, and the library's smoking policy does so.

But you may not ban a tenant from possessing cannabis or using it in other ways, such as edibles, and you may not require a tenant to take a drug test.

You may not refuse to rent to, or treat differently, someone because of a past conviction for possessing a small amount of cannabis, or solely because they are a qualifying medical cannabis patient or caregiver (from October 1, 2026, including a qualifying out-of-state patient or caregiver) unless federal law or federal funding requires it.

The possession, use, drug-test and conviction rules do not apply to a roomer who does not lease the whole home, a residence incidental to detention or to medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious or similar services, transitional or sober-living housing, or where federal law or a federal benefit requires a ban.

title: Tenant's Insurance and Your Repair Duties
bodyText: No Connecticut statute says whether you may require a tenant to make a claim on the tenant's renter's insurance. Two rules limit how far a lease can go: you remain responsible for the repairs and upkeep Connecticut law puts on landlords, and a lease cannot make a tenant release you from, or pay for, liability the law places on you. Do not make a tenant's insurance claim a condition of doing repairs you owe.

title: Wells, Septic and Water Testing
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant law doesn't name wells or septic systems, but you must keep the plumbing and sanitary facilities you supply in good and safe working order and supply running water and reasonable hot water, so treat keeping a private well or septic system working as your job. Before renting a home with a private well, you must also tell the tenant about the state's well-testing information (the library has a lease clause for this notice). In a single-family home you and the tenant may agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant will handle specified maintenance tasks, but that cannot be used to dodge your duties. Whenever water testing for the property shows a contaminant above the state limit, you must send a copy of the results to every tenant within 48 hours after you receive them.

title: Tenant Duties Under Connecticut Law
bodyText:
Connecticut law requires every tenant to: follow the building, housing and fire code duties that fall on tenants; keep the part of the premises they use as clean and safe as its condition allows; take garbage and waste to the place you provide; keep plumbing fixtures and appliances clean; use electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, air conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, reasonably; not deliberately or carelessly damage the property or let anyone else do so; not disturb neighbors or create a nuisance; and not let a household member who was evicted for selling drugs move back in without your consent.

If a tenant materially breaks these duties in a way that materially affects other tenants' health and safety or the physical condition of the property, you must first give a written notice ending the lease at least 15 days after receipt; a breach that can be fixed by repair or paying damages is cured if the tenant does so within that time. A serious nuisance, or letting an evicted drug-selling household member back in, can go straight to a notice to quit.

title: Which Utilities a Tenant Can Be Made to Pay
bodyText:
Make a tenant pay only for utilities measured by a separate meter for that tenant's unit alone.

By law you are responsible for electricity, gas, water and heating fuel supplied to the building unless the service is individually metered or billed for the exclusive use of one unit, and for leases signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, a lease term making a tenant pay for utilities billed to the tenant without a separate meter that measures only what is delivered to their unit is unenforceable.

The statutes don't say whether that rule also reaches a submeter you bill under the state's submetering law, so get legal advice before billing a tenant from a submeter.

If heat or utilities are included in the rent, you may not add a surcharge for them. If a shared-meter account in your name goes unpaid, tenants who take service in their own name may deduct those payments from rent.

title: No Utility Shutoffs by Landlords
bodyText: Connecticut gives you no right to cut off a tenant's electricity, gas, water or heat for nonpayment, even if you submeter or bill the tenant for it; use the court eviction process instead. Electric submetering is allowed only in limited buildings approved by the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority (for example, multifamily buildings powered by renewable energy or combined heat and power), at no more than the utility's rate for that class of customer, and never for common-area use. If you fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service you are required to supply, and the failure is not caused by conditions beyond your control, the tenant may, after notice to you, buy it and deduct the cost from rent, move to substitute housing with rent abated, or, if the failure is wilful, end the lease and recover up to two months' rent or double damages. Wilfully failing to furnish heat or utilities your lease requires is a crime in Connecticut, and a utility will not shut off service at your request unless the tenant signs an agreement or you swear the unit is vacant.

title: No Cutoff for Untransferred Utilities
bodyText: Connecticut has no rule letting you shut off utilities still in your name because the tenant did not move the account into their own name. Require the transfer in the lease and follow up, but if service stays in your name, keep paying or ask the utility to switch the account. If you fall behind on an account serving tenants, the utility must warn the tenants and let them take service in their own names, and they may then deduct what they pay from the rent. Wilfully failing to furnish heat or utilities your lease requires is a crime in Connecticut, and a utility will not shut off service at your request unless the tenant signs an agreement or you swear the unit is vacant.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarm Rules
bodyText: Connecticut's fire code requires smoke alarms in every residential building; in existing apartments, single-station alarms must be outside each sleeping area near the bedrooms and on every level, including the basement. Newer buildings need hard-wired alarms with battery backup (buildings permitted on or after October 1, 1985). Carbon monoxide alarms are required in one- and two-family homes built under permits issued on or after October 1, 2005, and may be required elsewhere by the building and fire codes. Keeping the required alarms installed and working is your code duty; in a single-family home you may agree in writing that the tenant tests them and changes batteries. Tampering with or removing a smoke alarm is a crime. Check with your local fire marshal for your building's exact requirements.

title: No Alarm Tampering Fee Rule
bodyText: No Connecticut statute authorizes a set fee for a tenant who removes or tampers with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, so the library does not offer one. Tampering with a smoke alarm is already a crime in Connecticut. You may recover your actual cost to repair or replace an alarm the tenant damaged or removed, including from the security deposit at move-out, and repeated tampering can be a lease violation.

title: Substitute Housing and Relocation Costs
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to house a tenant elsewhere during ordinary repairs. But if you fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service you are required to provide, and the failure isn't beyond your control, the tenant may move to substitute housing after 48 hours (right away if the same failure recurs within six months); the rent stops for that period and the tenant can recover the housing cost up to the rent abated, plus attorney's fees. If a town's code enforcement forces a tenant out, the town pays relocation benefits and can bill you and place a lien on your property, unless the displacement did not result from your failure to meet your repair duties.

title: Appliances You Do Not Supply
bodyText: You must keep in good and safe working order the appliances and facilities you supply, or are required by law to supply. Appliances the tenant owns are the tenant's responsibility. Be careful with appliances you leave in the unit, such as a refrigerator left by a prior tenant: if you let the tenant use it, a court may treat it as supplied by you, and a lease clause cannot excuse you from a duty the law places on you. If you don't want to maintain an item, remove it before move-in or list in writing only items the tenant owns.

title: No Balcony Inspection Mandate
bodyText: Connecticut has no law requiring periodic engineering inspections of balconies, decks, porches or exterior stairs in rental buildings. You still must keep the premises fit and safe, keep common areas safe, and meet building and fire codes. Inspect elevated wood structures regularly and fix rot, loose railings and failing supports promptly. Buildings with three or more units get a yearly fire marshal inspection, and your town may have its own inspection rules.

title: Rent After Condemnation
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute that expressly bars collecting rent after a unit is condemned or ordered vacated, but you should expect to collect little. A lease cannot let you collect rent for any period in which you are not meeting your duty to keep the unit fit and up to code, and rent stops when fire or other casualty substantially impairs the tenant's use. A fair rent commission can suspend rent until you make repairs, a court can order rent paid into court and reduced, and if the town's code enforcement forces the tenant out, you can be billed for the tenant's relocation payments unless the displacement was not caused by your failure to meet your repair and code duties.

title: Tenants' Repair Remedies in Connecticut
bodyText: Connecticut's statutes do not give tenants a general right to make repairs and deduct the cost from rent for ordinary repair problems. Their statutory remedies are: ending a lease longer than one month if you don't fix a material problem within 15 days of written notice; if you fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service you must supply, and the failure is not beyond your control, buying it and deducting the cost or moving to substitute housing with rent abated; no rent while fire or other casualty substantially impairs the unit; and, at least 21 days after complaining to the housing code agency, paying rent into court so a judge can order repairs and reduce the rent. None of these is available for a problem the tenant, the tenant's family or guests caused. A lease also cannot let you collect rent for any period in which you are not meeting your repair and code duties, and tenants may raise other defenses in court; don't count on collecting full rent while a code or repair problem goes unfixed. A lease cannot take these remedies away.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: You must make reasonable changes to your rules, policies, practices and services when a tenant or applicant with a disability needs them to have an equal chance to use and enjoy the home, such as an assigned accessible parking space or an exception to a no-pets rule for an assistance animal. You must also allow reasonable physical modifications the tenant needs, at the tenant's expense; where reasonable, you may require the tenant to restore the interior to its original condition, except for normal wear, when they leave. These rules cover learning disabilities and physical or mental disabilities. They do not apply when you rent rooms in a single-family home you live in, or a unit in a two-family home where you live in the other unit.

title: After a Fire or Disaster
bodyText:
Connecticut has no special statute for tenancies after a declared disaster; its casualty rule applies.

If fire or another casualty the tenant did not cause damages the home so much that the tenant's use is substantially impaired, no rent is owed while that lasts. The tenant may move out right away and end the lease by written notice within 14 days, or, if staying is lawful, stop using the damaged part and pay a reduced rent. If the lease ends, return the security deposit and any prepaid rent, counting rent from the date of the casualty.

During a declared emergency, Connecticut also bars leasing or renting any item in the chain of distribution at an unconscionably excessive price. It is not settled whether that reaches the rent for a home, so the cautious course is to avoid sharp rent increases in a declared emergency area.

title: Renting the Same Unit Twice
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute on renting the same unit or room to two tenants for the same period, and none setting a remedy when you cannot deliver possession on the start date. If it happens, the tenant who cannot move in has ordinary contract claims against you. The library's possession-delay clause sets what happens if the unit isn't ready; avoid signing a new lease until the current tenant has actually moved out or a firm move-out date is in writing.

title: Which Fire, Building and Housing Codes Apply
bodyText: Connecticut requires you to comply with the state's tenement and lodging house law and with every building and housing code that materially affects health and safety; if a town ordinance or a building or fire code demands more than the state landlord law, the stricter rule wins. The State Fire Safety Code, based on national model codes, applies to rental buildings other than one- and two-family private homes, though its smoke alarm rules reach those homes too, and its carbon monoxide alarm rules reach those built under a building permit for new occupancy issued on or after October 1, 2005, unless the code exempts them; the State Fire Prevention Code also regulates hazards such as fuel, gas and flammable materials. The local fire marshal inspects multifamily buildings each year and inspects one- and two-family homes for smoke alarms on a complaint or request. Ask your local building official and fire marshal which code editions apply to your building.

title: No Furnished Rental Rules
bodyText: Connecticut has no special rules for furnished rentals, and the security deposit limit is the same (two months' rent, or one month for a tenant 62 or older). List the furniture you provide in the lease or a signed inventory, and note its condition on the move-in walk-through checklist; you may deduct from the deposit for damage the tenant causes beyond normal use. Furnished stays of 30 days or less can be subject to the state's room occupancy tax.

title: Shifting Repairs and Chores to the Tenant
bodyText: In a single-family home, you and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant handles garbage removal, supplies the heat, water and hot water, and does specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, so long as the deal is made in good faith and not to escape your legal duties. In any other building, you may agree in writing only that the tenant does specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, and only if the work is not needed to bring the unit up to code or make it fit and habitable and the deal doesn't reduce what you owe other tenants. Your basic duties to meet codes and keep the home fit and habitable stay with you. List each task specifically in the lease.

title: No Habitability Presumptions
bodyText: No Connecticut statute presumes that you breached your repair duties, or took too long to fix something, in an eviction or repair case. Don't count on a court never shifting that burden to you. But in an eviction a tenant may raise any legal, equitable or constitutional defense, including that you are evicting in retaliation for a complaint to housing officials or a fair rent commission. Keep records of repair requests and when you fixed each problem.

title: Repair Duties Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A Connecticut lease cannot make a tenant give up the right to a fit, code-compliant home or the remedies the law gives tenants, cannot release you from liability the law places on you, and cannot let you collect rent for any period in which you are not meeting your repair duties. Such terms are unenforceable. The only lawful way to shift work to a tenant is a written, good-faith agreement for specified tasks, and in buildings other than single-family homes that can never cover work needed to make the unit fit or code-compliant.

title: Local Health and Housing Code Enforcement
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to hand out your local health district's rental rules, but local health and housing officials enforce minimum standards in rentals. They can order you to fix conditions that endanger life or health in a rented one- or two-family home or in a building with three or more households, and a tenant must first complain to the local housing or health agency before asking a court to have rent paid into court. The state Public Health Code also lets the local health director order you to fix a building in a dilapidated or filthy condition that may endanger the health of people living nearby. When you give a tenant your written bed bug inspection results, you must include the local health department's contact information. Check your town's housing code.

title: Heat and Hot Water
bodyText: You must supply running water, reasonable hot water at all times and reasonable heat, unless the unit's heat and hot water come from equipment under the tenant's sole control or from utility service connected directly to the tenant. In a single-family home, the tenant may agree in writing to supply heat and hot water. If you fail to supply required heat or hot water, the tenant may buy it and deduct the cost from rent, move to substitute housing after 48 hours with rent abated, or, if the failure is wilful, end the lease and recover damages. Connecticut treats an indoor temperature below 65 degrees in an occupied home as injurious to health, and if the lease requires you to furnish heat or utilities, wilfully failing to do so is a crime. A heating oil or propane supplier serving a tenant-occupied building must keep it at 65 degrees or warn you, the state and the local health officer before stopping deliveries, and a utility will not cut service at your request without the tenant's signed agreement or your notarized statement that the unit is vacant.

title: No Right to Fix It and Bill It as Rent
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute letting you fix a problem the tenant caused and add the cost to the rent. You may enter on reasonable notice to make necessary repairs, charge the tenant the reasonable cost of damage the tenant or their guests caused, and deduct unpaid damage costs from the security deposit when the tenancy ends. Do not label repair costs as rent: Connecticut rent means periodic payments, and an eviction for nonpayment must rest on unpaid rent. For a tenant's material breach, use the written 15-day notice to cure.

title: Extra Standards for Buildings With Three or More Units
bodyText: If your building houses three or more households who share halls, stairways or yards (or is a lodging or boarding house), Connecticut adds specific standards: keep the building clean, in good repair and with a roof that doesn't leak; provide garbage and rubbish receptacles; light all public halls at night; provide water on every occupied floor where public water is available; provide at least one toilet for every two units of two rooms or less and one for each larger unit, on the same floor, with a window or vent; every bedroom must have an outside window (or a prescribed interior sash window); and keep interior paint free of peeling or chipping that could harm health. The local health or housing agency enforces these rules and can order repairs.

title: Terms a Connecticut Lease Cannot Contain
bodyText: A Connecticut lease may not make the tenant: give up rights under the landlord-tenant laws or any statute or town ordinance (unless that law says the right may be waived); let you get a court judgment without a hearing (confession of judgment); release you from, or pay for, liability the law places on you; give up interest on the security deposit; let you remove the tenant without a court order; let you seize the tenant's belongings for rent; pay your attorney's fees above 15% of a money judgment; pay a late charge before the grace period ends, above the legal limit, or get a discount for paying within the grace period; pay a heat or utilities surcharge when heat or utilities are included; or, for leases signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, pay for utilities not measured by a separate meter for the unit. A lease also cannot let you collect rent while you are not meeting your repair duties. Any such term is unenforceable.

title: Pools at Rental Properties
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant law has no pool fence or pool notice rule for rentals. But a pool or spa at an apartment complex or other multi-unit property counts as a public pool under state health law; only a pool used at a single-family home (and not for business) is excluded. It is not settled whether a pool at a two-family home, or at a single-family home you rent out, falls under that exclusion, so ask your local health department before assuming it does. Public pools are classified by the Department of Public Health, which must approve plans before one is built or substantially altered. The Public Health Code requires, among other things, a person who knows pool operation and water chemistry on duty whenever the pool is open, daily water testing and records, a barrier at least four feet high with self-closing, self-latching gates around an outdoor pool, a "Warning—No Lifeguard on Duty" sign when no lifeguard is on duty, and a local permit or registration with the local health director. The local health director inspects public pools and can close one. Check with your local health department and building official before opening a pool to tenants.

title: Promises to Repair
bodyText: Connecticut has no rule that your promises to clean, repair or improve a unit be in writing or carry a completion date. Still, put any such promise in the lease or a signed addendum with a date: it then becomes a lease term you must keep, and a tenant may end a lease longer than one month if you materially fail to keep the lease and don't fix it within 15 days of written notice. You may enter on reasonable notice to make agreed repairs.

title: Respecting the Tenant's Possession
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute stating a covenant of quiet enjoyment. The state's court rules mention a claim for a landlord's breach of one, but its reach depends on court decisions, so assume your lease carries one. Several statutes also protect a tenant's possession. Enter only with the tenant's consent on reasonable notice, in an emergency, under a court order, or after the tenant abandons or surrenders the unit; an unlawful entry or repeated harassing demands cost at least one month's rent plus attorney's fees. Locking a tenant out or taking their belongings without a court order is a crime and can cost double damages. Wilfully failing to provide heat or utilities the lease requires is also a crime.

title: Rental Inspections
bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide rental license or inspection program, but towns may adopt housing codes for safe and sanitary housing and fine rental owners up to $2,000 per violation (violations found on the same date count as one). The local fire marshal inspects buildings with three or more units each year and may enter at reasonable hours; one- and two-family homes are inspected for smoke alarms on a complaint or request. A tenant must not unreasonably refuse you entry for inspections on reasonable notice, but no statute lets the lease itself authorize a government inspector to enter. Check your town's rental registration, licensing and inspection rules.

title: No Right to End the Lease Over Repair Costs
bodyText: Connecticut gives you no right to end a tenancy because a needed repair would cost too much. Your duty to keep the home fit and up to code applies regardless of cost. After a fire or other casualty, the tenant may end the lease, and the library offers an optional clause letting you end it too; otherwise you must repair, or end a month-to-month tenancy or let a lease expire with proper notice.

title: How Tenants Give Repair Notice
bodyText: You may ask tenants to make repair requests in writing, but Connecticut ties tenant remedies to different kinds of notice and a lease cannot take them away. A tenant who wants to end the lease for your failure to make repairs must give written notice. For heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service, reasonable oral notice is enough to start the tenant's remedies. Bed bugs may be reported orally or in writing. Before suing to pay rent into court, the tenant must have complained to the local housing or health code agency at least 21 days earlier. Act on every report you receive, however it arrives.

title: Locks and Rekeying
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring particular locks, deadbolts or door viewers in rentals, or rekeying between tenants; your town's housing code may. Rekeying at each turnover is still good practice. Connecticut does require you to change the locks, or let the tenant change them, within set deadlines when a tenant protected by a court order asks.

title: No Staff Work-Card Rule
bodyText: Connecticut has no law requiring work cards or background checks for maintenance or management staff in housing for older adults or in any other private rental housing. Screening staff who have keys to occupied units is still good practice; follow the state's rules on use of criminal records in employment decisions.

title: No State Stove or Refrigerator Requirement
bodyText: Connecticut statutes do not require you to supply a stove or refrigerator, but if you supply them you must keep them in good and safe working order. Your town's housing code may require cooking facilities, so check local rules. List the appliances you supply in the lease.

title: Receivership of Rents for Code Violations
bodyText: If your town has adopted Connecticut's receivership law and you don't obey a health or housing order to fix dangerous conditions, or you substantially fail your duty to keep the property fit and up to code, the town can ask the court to appoint a receiver to collect the rents and make the repairs. The town then gets a lien on the property, ahead of existing mortgages, for the receiver's costs. You or your lender can avoid a receiver by showing you can do the work promptly and posting security. Separately, an electric, gas or telephone company or a municipal utility you fail to pay can ask the court to have the rents paid to a receiver to cover service to the tenants.

title: Cable TV Access in Apartment Buildings
bodyText: If you own a building with several units, you must let a cable TV company wire the building when a tenant asks for service, as long as the company pays the full cost, indemnifies you for damage and follows state utility rules. You may not demand or accept payment for allowing cable service, except compensation the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority approves, and you may not charge different rent or provide different service to tenants who do or don't subscribe. If the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority finds a violation after a hearing, you can owe a civil penalty of up to $1,000 for each day you fail to comply after its final order. Federal rules may also protect a tenant's satellite dish in areas the tenant controls.

title: No Utility Allowance Overage Charges
bodyText: If the lease includes heat or a utility in the rent, a lease term making the tenant pay a heat or utilities surcharge is unenforceable. The law doesn't define "surcharge", but an extra charge when usage runs over an allowance likely counts, so the safe course is not to charge one. For leases signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, you also may not make a tenant pay for any utility that is not measured by a separate meter serving only the tenant's unit. If you want the tenant to bear usage costs, put the utility in the tenant's own name on an individual meter.

title: No Splitting of Shared Utility Bills
bodyText: For leases signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, a lease term making a tenant pay for utilities that are not measured by a separate meter for their unit is unenforceable, so you cannot split a shared utility bill among tenants by a formula such as square footage or number of occupants. Utilities supplied to the building are your responsibility to the utility unless a meter or separate billing serves only one unit. For earlier leases no statute addresses a lease term that splits a shared bill, so don't rely on one. Build shared-utility costs into the rent instead, and remember that recurring charges must be included in the advertised rent.

title: Learning of a Tenant Utility Shutoff
bodyText: Connecticut's utility shutoff rules let any customer ask the gas, electric or water utility, through the company's own procedure, to send copies of all shutoff notices to a third person the customer names. That person is not responsible for the bills unless they agreed to be. You can ask the tenant in the lease to name you as that third person, to show proof of payment on request, and to tell you promptly of any shutoff notice. Connecticut's utility protections run toward tenants: when an account is in your name, the utility must warn the occupants before cutting service for your nonpayment, and a utility will not cut service at your request without the tenant's signed agreement or your notarized statement that the unit is vacant.

title: Utilities Billed in Your Name
bodyText: If an electric, gas, telephone or water company or a municipal utility bills you for service to a tenant-occupied building and you fall behind, it must try to warn the tenants (a heating oil or propane supplier instead must keep the building at 65 degrees or give advance notice to you, the state and the local health officer) and let them take service in their own names, without paying your past-due balance or a deposit; if that isn't practical, it can't shut off service but may ask a court to send the rents to a receiver to pay for service. Tenants may deduct what they pay the utility from the rent, and you may not raise the rent to get it back. You are responsible for the electricity, gas, water and heating fuel supplied to the building except service metered or billed to a single unit for its occupants alone, and wilfully failing to provide heat or utilities the lease requires is a crime.

title: Utility Shutoff Protections
bodyText: Connecticut's utility shutoff rules bind utilities, not landlords, but they affect your tenants and your house accounts. Utilities may not cut service for nonpayment on a Friday, weekend, holiday or the day before one, or when their offices are closed. From November 1 through May 1, electric and gas-heat service may not be cut for a residential customer in financial hardship, and at any time service may not be cut where that would create a life-threatening situation for a household that cannot pay. Before a shutoff for nonpayment, the utility must mail at least 13 days' notice, must first offer a gas or electric residential customer a payment plan, and, if the account is in your name, must try to notify the tenants of their rights at least 13 days ahead. A utility will not cut service to a rented unit at your request unless the tenant signs an agreement or you swear the unit is vacant, and heating oil or propane suppliers must give notice before stopping deliveries to a tenant-occupied building.

title: Submetering Utilities
bodyText: Connecticut lets landlords submeter electricity only in limited situations approved by the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority, such as multifamily buildings powered by renewable energy or combined heat and power. An approved submetering entity may charge no more than the utility's rate for that class of customer and may never bill a tenant for common-area use. No Connecticut statute authorizes water submetering or prescribes a lease disclosure. Submetered electricity under the state program can be left out of the advertised rent, but any other recurring utility charge you bill must be in it. For leases signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, a tenant cannot be made to pay for a utility without a separate meter for the unit. An approved submeter measures only the unit's use, so it likely counts, but this is untested; get legal advice before relying on it.

title: Entering the Unit
bodyText:
A Connecticut tenant must not unreasonably refuse to let you in to inspect, make repairs or improvements, provide services, or show the unit to buyers, lenders, new tenants or contractors. You must give reasonable written or oral notice and come at reasonable times.

Without the tenant's consent you may enter only in an emergency, during a tenant's extended absence, under a court order, or after the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit.

If a tenant unreasonably refuses entry, you may go to court for an order or to end the tenancy and recover damages and attorney's fees. An unlawful entry, or repeated demands that harass the tenant, costs you at least one month's rent in damages plus attorney's fees.

title: No Smart-Lock Statute
bodyText: Connecticut has no law aimed at smart locks, keypads or app-based entry in rentals. The usual entry rules apply whatever the technology: an electronic entry log does not replace notice and the tenant's consent. If a tenant protected by a court order asks for a lock change, you may meet the duty by reprogramming a digital or electronic lock with a new code.

title: Handling an Abandoned Unit
bodyText:
Connecticut gives you a way to retake a unit all the occupants have abandoned without going to court, but only by following the statute exactly: send the notice by both regular and certified mail, wait ten days for a response, then inventory and store anything left for at least 30 days before disposing of it.

If you know or should know someone still lives there, you must use the court eviction process instead. A lease cannot give you a faster or easier procedure: Connecticut voids lease terms that waive tenant rights, let you remove a tenant without a court order, or let you seize a tenant's property for rent.

After a court eviction, a state marshal removes belongings to the town's storage, and the town may auction what isn't claimed within 15 days.

title: Re-Renting After a Tenant Leaves Early
bodyText: If a tenant abandons the unit before the lease ends, you must make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rent. If you don't, the law treats the lease as ended by you on the date you learned of the abandonment, which cuts off your claim for later rent. When you end a lease for the tenant's breach and sue, your damages include the rent agreed in the lease but unpaid, and you must still take reasonable steps to reduce your loss. Keep records of your advertising and showings.

title: Attorney's Fees in Connecticut
bodyText: Your lease may make a tenant pay your attorney's fees only in a lawsuit for money damages, and then no more than 15% of the judgment. You may not collect fees for work done before a lawsuit is filed, or for a lawyer who is your salaried employee. If your lease lets you recover attorney's fees, the tenant automatically gets the same right if the tenant wins a case based on the lease. Separately, several statutes let a tenant recover attorney's fees, for example for unlawful entry, failure to supply essential services, bed bug violations or advertising rent without required fees, and let you recover fees if a tenant unlawfully refuses entry.

title: Converting a Rental Building to Condominiums
bodyText: If you convert a rental building (or mobile home park) to condominiums or another common interest community, each tenant living there before and after the conversion gets strong protections. You must hand-deliver or send by certified mail a conversion notice at least nine months before the tenant must leave, and the tenant has 90 days to buy the unit; for nine months after that you may not offer it to anyone else at a better price or on better terms. During the transition period (until nine months after the notice or the end of the lease, whichever is later) you may not raise the rent or evict except for good cause, and the tenant may end the lease on 30 days' notice. Lower-income tenants who move are entitled to a relocation payment of two months' rent or $1,000, whichever is more. A lease clause letting you cancel the lease because of a conversion is unenforceable. Before creating the community you must register it and each unit with the Department of Housing, send the Department a copy of each conversion notice, and report afterward on what happened to the tenants. A tenant harmed by a violation, or by pressure meant to push them out, can sue for damages, a court order and attorney's fees. These protections do not apply to condominiums created before May 7, 1980, or other communities created before January 1, 1983.

title: Criminal Activity and Serious Nuisance
bodyText: Connecticut lets you skip the 15-day cure notice and go straight to a notice to quit when a tenant commits a "serious nuisance": hurting or credibly threatening another tenant or you, substantial deliberate destruction, conduct posing an immediate serious danger, or using or allowing the unit to be used for prostitution or illegal drug sales. If a household member is evicted for selling drugs there, the tenant may not let that person move back without your consent. If you know your property is being used for prostitution and make no reasonable effort to stop it, you can be prosecuted yourself, and repeated arrests for listed crimes at a property can lead the state to sue to abate it as a public nuisance. Connecticut has no statute on crime-free lease addenda, so use the lease's serious-nuisance clause rather than a separate addendum.

title: Notice Before Ending a Lease for a Breach
bodyText: For unpaid rent, you may serve a notice to quit once the nine-day grace period has passed (four days for a weekly tenancy, plus five more if your online payment system blocked the payment); no separate cure notice is needed. For other material lease or rule violations, or a tenant's breach of health and safety duties, you must first deliver a written notice describing the violation and stating the lease will end on a date at least 15 days after the tenant receives it.
