If the problem can be fixed by repairs or by paying for the damage and the tenant does so within those 15 days, the lease continues; if substantially the same violation happens again within six months, you can go straight to a notice to quit. A serious nuisance needs no cure notice. Every notice to quit must give at least three days, follow the statutory form and be served by a state marshal or other proper officer.

title: Drug-Free Addenda and Cannabis Limits
bodyText: No Connecticut statute requires or regulates a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum; the lease's serious-nuisance clause covers illegal drug sales. Be careful with drug rules, though: you may not ban tenants from possessing or using cannabis (you may ban smoking or vaping it), and you may not require a tenant to take a drug test. Those limits do not apply to a roomer renting part of a home, transitional housing or a sober living home, or where federal law or a federal subsidy requires a ban or testing. Federally assisted housing has its own required lease addenda.

title: Protections for Victims of Violence
bodyText: You may not refuse to rent to someone, or end or deny their housing, because they are a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or human trafficking, and you may not set different lease terms because someone is a victim of sexual assault or trafficking. Violations can lead to a complaint with the Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities and are a criminal misdemeanor. These rules do not apply to renting rooms in a single-family home you live in, or to a two-family home where you live in the other unit. Connecticut has no special eviction defense for victims, but you should not treat violence against a tenant, or a tenant's call for help, as the tenant's lease violation.

title: Early Termination by Victims of Violence
bodyText: A tenant who is a victim of family violence or sexual assault and reasonably fears imminent harm may end the lease early, with no penalty or liability for the rest of the term, by giving you written notice at least 30 days before the move-out date. The notice must include a sworn statement and either a police or court record dated within 90 days or a statement from the Office of Victim Services or Office of the Victim Advocate dated within 30 days. The tenant still owes rent due before the termination date and any damage they caused, and any co-tenants remain bound by the lease. Do not charge an early-termination fee in these cases. If you believe the notice does not meet the law's requirements, your remedy is to ask the housing court to block the termination.

title: Lock Changes for Tenants With Protective Orders
bodyText: If a tenant gives you a copy of a protective or restraining order that orders someone to stay away from the tenant or the tenant's home, and asks you to change the locks, you must tell the tenant within six hours whether you will change them or the tenant may. If you agree to do it, change them within 48 hours and give the tenant a new key; otherwise the tenant may change them and must give you a key within two business days. You may charge only the actual reasonable cost of the lock and locksmith, and you may collect it by suit or from the deposit at move-out, but never by eviction. If the person ordered to stay away is a co-tenant, do not give them a key or let them in without a court order; they still owe rent, and you may not charge the protected tenant extra rent or fees because of the exclusion.

title: Property Taken by Eminent Domain
bodyText: Connecticut does not end a lease automatically when a government takes the property by eminent domain. If the taking destroys the property's value for the purpose it was leased, the court in the condemnation case may cancel the lease, end the rent and divide the award on that basis; otherwise your lease and court decisions control. If you want the lease to end on a taking, say so in the lease, and do not claim the tenant's share of any award unless the lease gives it to you. In the condemnation case, the court may value the whole property and divide the award so the tenant receives the income for the rest of the term, still subject to rent. A tenant forced to move by a state or local project is usually entitled to relocation payments and help from the acquiring agency.

title: Stays After an Eviction Judgment
bodyText: Winning an eviction case does not mean immediate possession. Connecticut automatically stays execution for five days after judgment (not counting Sundays and legal holidays), and an appeal filed in that time delays it further, though the court can require the tenant to pay use and occupancy during the appeal. Except in farm-worker or employee housing, seasonal resort rentals and transient lodging, a tenant evicted for a reason other than nonpayment, nuisance, illegal or immoral use, or occupying without ever having a right to, may ask the court for up to six months to find another home; for nonpayment, the tenant can get up to three months only by paying the full arrearage to the court within five days. The court can require the tenant to keep paying use and occupancy during any stay. No lease term can waive or limit these stays.

title: How a Connecticut Eviction Works
bodyText: You can remove a tenant only through a court "summary process" case; changing the locks, removing belongings or shutting off utilities without a court order can cost you double damages and is a crime. Start with a written notice to quit in the statutory form giving at least three days, served by a state marshal, with the court's right-to-counsel notice attached. After that date passes, a marshal serves the summons and complaint; if the tenant doesn't appear you can move for a default judgment, and if the tenant does appear you can ask the court to order use-and-occupancy payments while the case is pending. Starting January 1, 2027, in nonpayment cases you must give the tenant your latest lease with all addenda and the rent ledger by the first court date. Taking rent you know is overdue waives your right to evict for that missed payment, so accept later payments only "for use and occupancy" with the statutory disclaimer.

title: Eviction Records You Cannot Use
bodyText: When an eviction case is withdrawn, dismissed or decided for the tenant, the Judicial Branch removes it from its public website within 30 days. Once removed, no one may disclose that record for any commercial purpose, which the law defines to include tenant screening reports and any use related to screening applicants; it is not settled whether that also bars you from using a removed record yourself, so the safe course is not to use it in your own decision about whether to rent. Cases you won are not removed and may still be considered, subject to fair housing law. Make sure any screening company you use excludes removed cases, and do not rely on old printouts or third-party copies of them.

title: Good Cause for Older and Disabled Tenants
bodyText: Connecticut has no general just-cause eviction law: you can let a lease end at its term, or end a month-to-month tenancy with a proper notice to quit, without giving a reason, as long as you are not retaliating or discriminating. There is one big exception. In a building or complex with five or more units, or a mobile home park, a tenant who is 62 or older or has a physical or mental disability expected to last at least 12 months or to result in death, or who permanently lives with a spouse, sibling, parent or grandparent who is 62 or older or with a spouse, sibling, child, parent or grandparent who has such a disability, can be evicted only for nonpayment, refusing a fair and equitable rent increase, serious lease, rule or health-and-safety violations, a lease made void by the tenant's conviction for keeping the unit as a house of prostitution or lewdness, or for illegal gambling there, permanently removing the unit from the rental market, or your good-faith plan to live in the unit yourself; refusing a rent increase, removal from the market and moving in yourself cannot be used during an existing lease term. In a condominium or other common interest community this applies only to conversion tenants (against whom the move-in ground is unavailable) or where you own five or more units there. Rent increases for these tenants must be fair and equitable and can be challenged before a fair rent commission or in court. You may ask a tenant claiming protection for proof, which the tenant must provide within 30 days.

title: Protected-Tenant Notice for Larger Buildings
bodyText: If your building or complex has five or more units (or you run a mobile home park with five or more homes), you must give every tenant the Department of Housing's notice of the special eviction and rent-increase protections for tenants who are 62 or older or have a long-term disability. Give it when you first rent the unit and again every time the lease is renewed, to every tenant, whether or not you think they qualify. Use the Department's one-page form (DOH Form AM-011), which is available in English and Spanish on its website. Keep a signed or dated copy with the lease as proof you delivered it.

title: Tenants When a Rental Is Foreclosed
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to tell tenants that your lender has started a foreclosure, but your tenants keep strong rights if the foreclosure goes through. A new owner who takes the property by foreclosure generally must honor a genuine, arms-length lease for its remaining term and give at least 90 days' written notice to vacate; a month-to-month tenant also gets 90 days. The lease can end earlier only if the new owner sells to a buyer who will live there, still with 90 days' notice, and a Housing Choice Voucher tenant's lease and housing assistance contract carry over. If a foreclosing lender or buyer offers money to get a tenant to leave, the offer must be at least the deposit plus interest, two months' rent or $2,000, whichever is greatest.

title: Lease Guarantors
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute specific to lease guarantors. A guaranty must be in writing and signed by the guarantor to be enforceable. No statute limits a guarantor to the original lease term, so whether the guarantor is bound for renewals depends on what the guaranty says; if you want coverage for renewals and month-to-month extensions, say so expressly and have the guarantor sign. Do not use a guarantor to collect more up-front money than the security deposit limit allows, since the law does not say whether a deposit taken from a guarantor counts toward that limit.

title: No Waiver of Collection Exemptions
bodyText: Do not put a clause in your lease asking the tenant to waive the homestead exemption or the exemptions that protect household goods, wages and benefits from collection. Connecticut has no law allowing such a waiver, and a lease term that gives up a tenant's statutory rights is unenforceable unless the statute itself says its rights can be waived. Connecticut also forbids lease terms that let you seize a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent. If you win a money judgment, collect it through the court's ordinary execution process, subject to the exemptions.

title: Moving to Care or Senior Housing
bodyText: Connecticut gives tenants no statutory right to end a lease early because of age, illness, disability or a move to a nursing home, assisted living or senior housing. If a tenant with a disability asks to be released early because of that disability, treat it as a reasonable-accommodation request under fair housing law and consider it seriously. If the tenant simply leaves, you must still make reasonable efforts to re-rent the unit, which limits what you can recover. A month-to-month tenant can always end the tenancy with proper notice.

title: No Landlord's Lien on Tenant Property
bodyText: Connecticut does not give residential landlords a lien on a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent, and a lease clause letting you seize or hold the tenant's property for rent is unenforceable. Keeping a tenant's belongings, or keeping the tenant from reaching them, without a court order is a crime and can make you liable for double damages. To collect unpaid rent, sue and enforce the judgment through the court, where some of the tenant's property is exempt. Belongings left in the unit are handled only through the abandonment procedure, the death-of-tenant procedure or a marshal's removal after an eviction judgment.

title: Possession and Money Claims When a Lease Ends
bodyText: In Connecticut an eviction (summary process) case gets you possession of the unit and your court costs; to collect unpaid rent or damages for the tenant's breach, you bring an action for damages (whether it can be joined to the eviction case is a court-practice question). Those damages include the rent agreed to but unpaid, but you must make reasonable efforts to re-rent the unit to reduce your loss. While an eviction case is pending you can ask the court to order the tenant to pay use and occupancy into court each month. A lease clause making the tenant pay your attorney's fees is limited to 15 percent of any money judgment.

title: Agreed Damages and Early-Termination Charges
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant statutes do not address a lease term fixing in advance what a tenant owes for breaking the lease. Your damages for a breach include the agreed rent that goes unpaid, and you must try to re-rent the unit to reduce them. A separate consumer-contract law makes an agreed-damages clause in a written consumer contract for goods or services unenforceable unless the tenant signs or initials a boldface acknowledgment right after it; it is not settled whether that law covers a residential lease. A clause that works as a penalty is not enforceable either way, and you may not charge a move-out fee. Get legal advice before adding an agreed-damages or early-termination charge.

title: No Lockouts for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: You may not change the locks, shut off access or remove a tenant's belongings because rent is unpaid, even if the lease says you may. A lease term letting you remove a tenant without a court order is unenforceable in Connecticut. Keeping a tenant out of the unit or away from their belongings without a court order is the crime of criminal lockout, and the tenant can also sue for entry and detainer and recover double damages. To regain possession, serve a notice to quit and bring a summary process (eviction) case; only a state marshal acting on a court execution may remove the tenant.

title: Minors in Eviction Cases
bodyText: You do not need to name a tenant's minor children in a Connecticut eviction case: the judgment binds the named defendants and any minors holding under them. No statute forbids naming a minor, but if you do, the court may order the minor's name struck from the case record and removed from the Judicial Branch website. The safer practice is to name only the adult tenants and occupants.

title: Notice to Quit for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Connecticut has no separate pay-or-quit notice. If rent is still unpaid nine days after it is due (four days in a week-to-week tenancy, and five more days in a month when your online payment system kept the tenant from paying), you may end the tenancy by a written notice to quit in the statutory form, served by a state marshal, giving at least three days before the date to move out. Attach the Judicial Branch's one-page right-to-counsel notice to the notice to quit and to the eviction summons and complaint. If you knowingly accept overdue rent, you waive the right to end the tenancy for that late payment; after the notice to quit, accept money only as use and occupancy, using the statutory disclaimer.

title: Public Nuisance Actions Against a Rental Property
bodyText: Only the state (a state's attorney) can sue to abate a public nuisance at a Connecticut rental, and only after three or more arrests, arrest warrants showing a pattern, or listed municipal citations for listed offenses on the property within the past 365 days. Listed offenses include drug sales, prostitution, gambling, illegal liquor sales, serious assaults, firearm offenses and fire-code violations. The court can order repairs, appoint a receiver to collect the rents, or close the property, and can charge a liable owner the costs, including relocating uninvolved tenants. An owner who cooperates in good-faith efforts to abate the nuisance is exempted as a defendant, and an owner sued can defend by showing reasonable steps that did not succeed, so act promptly on criminal activity, including by eviction where the law allows.

title: Ending a Lease to Move In
bodyText: Connecticut law gives you no right to end a fixed-term lease early because you or a relative want to move in. A lease can end on a condition the lease itself states, so a clause reserving that right is not forbidden, but this library does not offer one: courts may refuse to enforce it on equitable grounds, and it cannot be used during the term against a tenant in a building or complex of five or more units or a mobile home park who is 62 or older or has a disability expected to last at least 12 months or to result in death, or who permanently lives with a spouse, sibling, parent or grandparent who is 62 or older or a spouse, sibling, child, parent or grandparent with such a disability (in a condominium or other common interest community, only conversion tenants or where you own five or more units there). For those tenants, a good-faith plan to make the unit your principal residence is a ground for eviction only after the lease term ends, and never against a conversion tenant in a condominium or other common interest community. Get legal advice before adding your own clause.

title: No End-of-Term Possession Bond
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute letting a tenant give a bond to deliver possession at the end of the term, and a lease may not let you confess judgment against the tenant. If a tenant stays after the lease ends, use the notice to quit and summary process (or the end-of-term notice waiver, if the lease has one).

title: Late Delivery of Possession
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute that says what happens if you cannot hand over the unit on the lease start date. The lease's possession-delay section governs: no rent is owed until you deliver possession, and the tenant may cancel and get back everything paid if the delay runs past 30 days. Other remedies turn on general contract law.

title: Tenant's Belongings After an Eviction
bodyText: In Connecticut only a state marshal, acting on a summary process execution after any stay ends, may remove an evicted tenant and their belongings. The marshal notifies the town's chief executive officer, serves the execution on the occupants at least 24 hours before the removal, and delivers the belongings to the town's designated storage place; you do not store them yourself. You pay the marshal for the removal and can recover that cost from the tenant. If the tenant does not reclaim the belongings and pay storage within 15 days, the town sells them at auction. A person who stays after the marshal returns and refuses to leave may be arrested for criminal trespass.

title: Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute letting a tenant end a nonpayment eviction just by paying before judgment, but if you knowingly accept overdue rent, you give up the right to evict for that late payment. After the notice to quit, accept money only as use and occupancy, with the statutory disclaimer. After a nonpayment judgment, the tenant may deposit the full arrearage with the court clerk within five days and then ask for a stay of execution; for nonpayment, stays may total no more than three months and usually require ongoing use and occupancy payments. A lease term waiving the tenant's stay rights is void.

title: Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: In a Connecticut eviction case the tenant may raise any legal, equitable or constitutional defense without first paying rent into court. Once the tenant appears, you can move for an order that the tenant deposit use and occupancy (the last agreed rent) with the court each month; if the tenant does not pay as ordered, the court can move quickly to judgment. Separately, a tenant who has complained to the housing code agency at least 21 days earlier can sue you to enforce repairs and must pay each month's rent to the court clerk; while that rent is deposited you cannot evict for nonpayment, and the court can use the money for repairs. Appeals also require use and occupancy payments.

title: No Retaliation Against Tenants
bodyText: For six months after a tenant in good faith complains to a state or local official or a fair rent commission about a code violation, asks you for repairs, files a housing-code action in court, or organizes or joins a tenants' union (or after a municipal agency issues a notice or order about a violation), you may not bring an eviction, demand a rent increase or cut the tenant's services. You may still evict for nonpayment, illegal use or a lease violation, to move into the unit yourself immediately and in good faith, if the tenant willfully caused the condition, or on a periodic-tenancy termination notice given before the complaint. You may raise rent if the tenant's lack of care caused the condition, or to pass through your prorated share of a substantial tax or operating-cost increase (not tied to fixing the complaint) that you became liable for at least four months before the demand. Separately, a tenant can defend any eviction by showing you brought it solely because the tenant tried to remedy a code violation.

title: No Self-Help Eviction
bodyText: In Connecticut the only lawful way to remove a tenant is a notice to quit, a summary process judgment and a state marshal's execution. Changing locks, removing doors or belongings, or otherwise keeping a tenant out without a court order is criminal lockout, and the tenant can sue for entry and detainer and recover double damages and costs. If you are required to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity or gas and willfully fail to do so, the tenant may end the lease and recover up to two months' rent or double actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. Entering the unit unlawfully or to harass costs at least one month's rent in damages.

title: Servicemember Tenants
bodyText: Connecticut has no state law letting a servicemember end an apartment or house lease early; the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act gives that right and its eviction protections, and the lease cannot take them away. (Connecticut's only state military termination right is for residents of mobile manufactured home parks.) Before a court enters a default judgment against a tenant who has not appeared, you must file an affidavit saying whether the tenant is in military service, and the court may appoint an attorney or stay the case. You may not refuse to rent to someone, or set different terms, because of their status as a veteran.

title: No Late-Benefit Eviction Defense
bodyText: Connecticut has no special eviction defense, continuance or stay for a tenant who fell behind because a Social Security or other benefit payment arrived late. The ordinary rules apply: the nine-day grace period, the notice to quit, and, after a nonpayment judgment, a stay of up to three months if the tenant first deposits the full arrearage with the clerk.

title: When a Tenant May End the Lease Early
bodyText: Connecticut lets a tenant end a lease early, whatever the lease says, in these cases: (1) the tenant or a dependent is a victim of family violence or sexual assault and the tenant gives 30 days' written notice with the sworn statement and records the law requires; (2) in a lease of more than one month, you materially breach the lease or a health-and-safety repair duty and do not fix it within 15 days after written notice; (3) you willfully fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service you must supply; (4) fire or other casualty not caused by the tenant substantially impairs the unit, and the tenant moves out and notifies you within 14 days; or (5) you enter unlawfully or repeatedly demand entry to harass the tenant. A tenant ending the lease for family violence or sexual assault still owes rent already past due and any damage they caused.

title: When the Lease Term Ends
bodyText:
A Connecticut lease can end on its last day, but if the tenant does not move out you must still serve a notice to quit (unless the lease validly waives it for the end of the term) and win a summary process case; you cannot remove the tenant or their belongings yourself.

A tenant who is 62 or older or has a disability expected to last at least 12 months or to result in death (or permanently lives with a spouse, sibling, parent or grandparent who is 62 or older, or a spouse, sibling, child, parent or grandparent with such a disability), in a building or complex of five or more units or a mobile home park, cannot be evicted just because the term ended (in a condominium or other common interest community, only conversion tenants or where you own five or more units there): you need one of the reasons the good-cause law lists.

A tenant staying on after the term does not by itself create a new lease.

title: Tenancies Without a Set Term
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant statutes do not recognize a separate residential "tenancy at will". If the rental agreement does not fix a definite term, the tenancy is month to month, or week to week if the tenant pays rent weekly, and an oral lease at a monthly rent with no agreed end date is a lease for one month. Without any agreement on rent, the tenant owes the fair rental value. To end such a tenancy you serve a notice to quit, and the good-cause rules for older and disabled tenants in larger buildings still apply.

title: When a Sole Tenant Dies
bodyText:
Connecticut does not end a lease automatically when a tenant dies.

If the only occupant under a monthly or fixed-term lease dies, and you have followed any lease term allowing termination on the occupant's death, you may use a special procedure instead of an eviction: mail notice (regular and certified) to the emergency contact the tenant named, if any, and to known next of kin; file an affidavit with the Probate Court; at least 30 days later inventory the belongings and file the inventory; wait 15 days before removing them, then store them securely for 15 more days.

If they are not reclaimed within the 60 days, the Probate Court certificate can be filed in Superior Court, where it counts as an eviction judgment, and a state marshal removes the belongings to the town's storage.

If someone applies to probate the estate within 55 days of your affidavit, you must stop. Following the procedure protects you from a lockout (entry and detainer) claim.

title: Ending a Month-to-Month Tenancy
bodyText:
Connecticut has no statute requiring 30 days' notice to end a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy.

You end it by a written notice to quit in the statutory form, served by a state marshal at least three days before the date the tenant must leave, with the Judicial Branch right-to-counsel notice attached; no statute says whether the quit date must fall at the end of a rental period, so it is safest to set it there.

No statute says how much notice a tenant must give you, so put it in the lease.

You may not end the tenancy of a tenant in a building or complex of five or more units or a mobile home park who is 62 or older or has a disability expected to last at least 12 months or to result in death, or who permanently lives with a spouse, sibling, parent or grandparent who is 62 or older or a spouse, sibling, child, parent or grandparent with such a disability, except for a reason the good-cause law lists (in a condominium or other common interest community, only conversion tenants or where you own five or more units there), and for six months after a tenant's good-faith complaint to housing officials, repair request or similar protected act you may not bring an eviction unless a statutory exception applies (for example nonpayment of rent, a good-faith move into the unit as your own home, or a termination notice you gave before the complaint).

A rent increase needs written notice of at least one full rental period for a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy (45 days for a longer term).

title: Removing a Squatter or Unauthorized Occupant
bodyText: Connecticut has no fast-track for removing squatters or a tenant's guest who will not leave. Someone who never had a right to occupy the unit is removed the same way as a tenant: a notice to quit served by a state marshal (you may address an occupant whose name you do not know as 'John Doe'), then a summary process case and execution. Name and serve every occupant you know of, because an execution cannot be enforced until it has issued against all occupants. Police may treat a person who knows they have no right to be there and refuses an order to leave as a criminal trespasser, but removing anyone yourself without a court order risks a criminal lockout charge if the person turns out to be a tenant.

title: Agreed Ways to Give Notice
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant statutes have no "actual notice" rule and no provision for the parties to agree on an extra notice method such as text messages. Notice of entry may be written or oral, so long as it is reasonable. A lease may say how routine notices are given, but an agreed method can never replace the steps a statute requires, such as service of a notice to quit by a state marshal or the mailings the abandonment and deceased-tenant procedures require.

title: Claims Against the Property
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring a tenant to tell you about a foreclosure, tax proceeding or other claim against the property, and no statute on a tenant recognizing someone else as landlord. Any such duty exists only if the lease creates it. If the property is foreclosed, a bona fide tenant keeps statutory protection against quick removal by the new owner.

title: Automatic Renewal Clauses
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant statutes say nothing about lease clauses that renew automatically. Two consumer laws regulate automatic renewals in contracts for consumer goods or services, requiring conspicuous disclosure, an annual reminder (since July 1, 2026) and, for contracts longer than 180 days, a written reminder 15 to 60 days before renewal explaining how to cancel, with violations treated as unfair trade practices; it is unsettled whether either applies to a residential lease. This library offers no automatic-renewal clause; a tenant who stays after the term is simply a holdover, and any rent increase still needs 45 days' written notice. If you want an automatic renewal, make it conspicuous and send the reminder, and get legal advice.

title: Other Rules Connecticut Does Not Have
bodyText: Three rules some states have do not exist in Connecticut law. (1) No statute bans renting the same unit to two tenants for the same period or gives a special remedy for it; contract and consumer-protection law apply. (2) No statute makes smoke-alarm compliance inadmissible in an injury case or limits insurers over it. (3) No statute gives a private landlord a special right to end a lease because the rental application was false (state-assisted public housing has its own rule); the lease's application-accuracy section makes a material falsehood a breach.

title: Squatters and Other Questions Outside the Landlord-Tenant Law
bodyText: (1) There is no squatter-specific removal procedure; someone who never had a right to occupy is removed by notice to quit and summary process. (2) There is no statewide rental license or registration you must hold to win an eviction; a town may require a nonresident owner to file a residential address, and failing to file is an infraction, not a bar to eviction. Business filings are different: an out-of-state limited liability company or corporation transacting business in Connecticut may not maintain a court case, an eviction included, until it registers with, or obtains a certificate of authority from, the Secretary of the State; owning property, without more, is not transacting business, so whether renting it out is depends on the facts and case law (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 34-275a(b), 34-275d(a)(10), 33-920(b)(9) and 33-921(a)). And renting under a name other than your own requires a trade name certificate from the town clerk, on pain of a fine of up to $500 or up to 1 year in prison, though the statute sets no bar on suing (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 35-1a(a) and 35-1d(d)). (3) Unlike some states, Connecticut does require you to give a written receipt for every cash payment, stating the date, amount and purpose. Towns may have their own registration or licensing rules.

title: Domestic Violence Citations Check
bodyText: Connecticut has not moved its protective-order laws. The lock-change statute still correctly cites restraining orders (section 46b-15), civil protection orders (46b-16a), family violence protective orders (46b-38c), standing criminal protective orders (53a-40e), stalking and sexual-assault protective orders (54-1k) and registered foreign orders (46b-15a). The early-termination statute for sexual-assault victims cites a spousal sexual-assault section 'revised to January 1, 2019' because that section was repealed later that year; the reference is intentional. Quote the definitions in those statutes rather than older guidance.

title: Electronic Leases, Signatures and Notices
bodyText: Connecticut's Uniform Electronic Transactions Act lets you and a tenant sign the lease and keep records electronically, but only if both of you have agreed to do business electronically, and a tenant who agrees once may refuse for other transactions. The Act does not cover notices of default, eviction or the right to cure under a lease of someone's primary residence, so give those on paper as the statutes require (a notice to quit must be served by a state marshal). An electronic record is presumed not received if you know the tenant did not receive it or could not open it.

title: Calls for Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute that expressly protects a tenant's right to call the police or emergency services or bars a lease penalty for such calls. Do not penalize those calls anyway: the anti-retaliation law protects tenants who contact officials about code violations, and fair housing law forbids refusing to rent to someone because they are a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or trafficking. This library's serious-nuisance clause promises not to treat a request for police or emergency help as a violation.

title: Pre-Suit Dispute Clauses
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute authorizing or regulating lease clauses that require the parties to try informal resolution or mediation before going to court. In the Hartford, New Britain, New Haven, Bridgeport, Waterbury and Stamford-Norwalk judicial districts, housing cases go to the court's housing docket, where housing mediators screen contested cases and can recommend settlements. A lease term that makes a tenant jump through extra steps before using a statutory remedy may be unenforceable, because a lease cannot make a tenant waive rights under the landlord-tenant statutes. This library does not offer a pre-suit clause.

title: No State Insurance Mandate
bodyText: Connecticut law does not require residential landlords to carry liability insurance, and there is no state rental registration tied to insurance. Your lender, condominium association or town may require coverage. A tenant who installs an electric vehicle charging station must carry a general liability policy naming you as an additional insured.

title: Rental Registration and Local Filings
bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide landlord registration or rental license. If you do not live in Connecticut, your town may require you to file your current residential address (not a post office box) with the assessor or another office; if you own through a company, the filing gives the residential address of your agent in charge and of each person with day-to-day financial or operational control. Report any change within 21 days. Failing to file is an infraction, and the town may impose civil penalties of up to $500 for a first violation and $1,000 after that; the town may serve code orders at the address on file. Towns may also license short-term rentals and, in buildings of three or more units, require a new certificate of occupancy after each vacancy, so check local ordinances. Two general business filings can also apply. If you rent under a name other than your own legal name, you need a trade name certificate from the town clerk where the business is principally transacted, or face a fine of up to $500 or up to 1 year in prison (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 35-1a and 35-1d(d)). And an out-of-state LLC or corporation transacting business here must register with, or get a certificate of authority from, the Secretary of the State, or it cannot maintain an eviction (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 34-275a and 33-921; see "Out-of-State Landlords").

title: No Crime-Free Lease Statute
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring or regulating crime-free lease addenda, and none requiring you to give police or child-protection investigators access or information. The rules that do apply limit such terms: eviction for criminal conduct runs through the serious-nuisance and lease-violation grounds, a lease cannot ban lawful cannabis possession (only smoking or vaping it), and fair housing law protects victims of domestic violence. Use this library's optional serious-nuisance clause rather than a separate crime-free addendum. One general reporting duty does bind you as it binds anyone: law enforcement officers, physicians and other persons must promptly notify the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner of any violent, sudden and unexpected, or suspicious death that comes to their attention, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit, and in an apparent homicide or suicide, or an accidental death of obscure cause, the scene must be left undisturbed until the medical examiner authorizes otherwise; a wilful failure carries a fine of up to $500, up to 1 year in prison, or both (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 19a-406(a) and 19a-407). Reporting child or elder abuse is mandatory only for listed professionals, though anyone may report suspected child abuse (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 17a-101a, 17a-103(a) and 17b-451).

title: No Statutory Rule on Blank Spaces
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in or treating a blank as a breach. The standardized rental terms summary form that must be the first page of every written lease must be completed, though. Fill in or strike every blank before anyone signs, so the lease cannot be read against you.

title: Giving the Tenant a Copy of the Lease
bodyText: No Connecticut statute requires you to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, and not doing so is not a statutory defense to enforcing it. Several related documents are required: the completed rental terms summary form as the first page of any written lease, signed duplicate walk-through checklists if the tenant asks for a walk-through, the protected-tenant notice for buildings of five or more units, a receipt for every cash payment, and a copy of the tenant's ledger on request. Give each tenant a full signed copy of the lease anyway; it also proves the tenant had notice of your rules.

title: No Initials Requirement
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant statutes never require a tenant to initial a particular lease term, including a longer notice period. If you add an agreed-damages or early-termination charge, a consumer-contract law may require a boldface acknowledgment the tenant signs or initials (whether it covers leases is unsettled). Initials remain good evidence that the tenant saw a key term, such as a waiver of the notice to quit at the end of the term.

title: Lease Length and Formalities
bodyText: Connecticut sets no maximum length for a residential lease, but how the lease is made limits it. An oral lease at a monthly rent with no agreed end date is a lease for one month, and any tenancy without a definite term is month to month (week to week if rent is weekly). An oral lease of one year or less is enforceable once the tenant moves in; a longer lease must be in writing and signed by the party it is enforced against. A lease for more than one year, or one with a renewal or purchase option, binds a buyer or lender only if the lease or a notice of lease is executed, witnessed, acknowledged and recorded on the land records like a deed.

title: Out-of-State Landlords
bodyText: If you are not a Connecticut resident and hold a tenant's security deposit, the security deposit statute requires you to appoint the Connecticut Secretary of the State, in writing, as your attorney to receive service of process in any lawsuit against you. You do not have to name an in-state agent in the lease, and tenants do not withhold tax from rent paid to you. Even without that written appointment, a nonresident individual who owns Connecticut real property is deemed to have appointed the Secretary of the State as agent for service of process in suits arising from it, so a tenant can sue you by serving the Secretary and mailing you a copy (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-59b(a)(4) and (c)). If you own through an out-of-state LLC or corporation that transacts business here, it must register with, or get a certificate of authority from, the Secretary of the State; until it does it cannot maintain an eviction or any other court case and owes $300 for each month unregistered after a 90-day grace period, and an unregistered LLC is treated as having appointed the Secretary as its agent for service. Owning property, without more, is not transacting business, so whether renting it out is depends on the facts and case law (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 34-275a, 34-275d(a)(10), 33-920(b)(9) and 33-921). Like every landlord, you must tell the tenant in writing, by the start of the tenancy, the name and address of the person managing the property and the person authorized to receive notices and legal papers, and your town may require you to file your residential address.

title: Extra Terms in Move-Out Notices
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute governing a move-out notice form you ask a tenant to sign, and no required warning if the form adds terms the lease does not contain. Keep such a form to the move-out date and forwarding address: a new term in it is only a proposed change the tenant must knowingly agree to, and it cannot waive any right the landlord-tenant statutes give the tenant.

title: Where Connecticut Law Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Several Connecticut rules depend on what the lease says, and a silent lease takes the default. (1) Rent is due at the unit, at the start of each month, unless the lease says otherwise. (2) You may charge a late charge only if the lease has a valid written late-charge term. (3) The tenant must tell you about an extended absence unless the lease says otherwise. (4) The tenant may use the unit only as a home unless you agree otherwise. (5) If you sell to a good-faith buyer and give the tenant written notice, you are released from later obligations unless the lease says otherwise. (6) A tenant may take on specified repairs only under a written good-faith agreement (in a single-family home, also trash and heat or hot water). (7) A written lease may waive the notice to quit at the end of the term. (8) The deceased-tenant procedure works best when the lease allows termination on the sole occupant's death. (9) In a converted condominium, a one-year lease signed after the conversion notice may waive the tenant's relocation payment after the transition period.

title: Rules That Depend on Size
bodyText: Connecticut has no general small-landlord exemption; each rule sets its own size test. Good-cause eviction protection for tenants 62 or older or with a disability, and the notice about it, apply in a building or complex of five or more units (a complex counts buildings on the same or adjoining lots under the same owner) or a mobile home park; in a condominium or other common interest community the protection reaches conversion tenants whatever you own, and other tenants only if you own five or more units there. A tenant's right to install an electric vehicle charger phased in by how many units you own in total, and does not apply where there are fewer than five parking spaces. Single-family residences may shift trash and heat duties to the tenant by written agreement. The bed bug statute does not cover single-family unattached units. A town may require a new certificate of occupancy after each vacancy in buildings of three or more units. Fair housing law exempts renting rooms in your own single-family home and units in an owner-occupied two-family house, and allows an owner-occupied building of up to four units to decline families with children.

title: Renter's Insurance Is Unregulated
bodyText: Connecticut neither requires renter's insurance nor limits your ability to require it in the lease, and it sets no rules on which insurer the tenant uses, proof deadlines or force-placed coverage. A lease cannot, however, make the tenant release you from liability the law places on you or indemnify you for it, so an insurance requirement cannot shift your own legal responsibilities to the tenant. Insurers, not landlords, must give renters a notice about flood coverage.

title: Selling or Changing Management of a Rented Property
bodyText: When you sell a rented Connecticut property to a good-faith buyer, you are released from lease obligations for later events only after you give the tenant written notice of the sale, unless the lease says otherwise; a manager is released for events after its management ends. The new owner must give each tenant, when it takes over, the name and address of the manager and of the person authorized to receive notices and legal papers. You must hand over the tenants' security deposits, with interest earned, to the buyer, who becomes liable for returning them; whoever holds a deposit must tell the tenant in writing, within 30 days, the amount and the name and address of the bank holding it. You may show the unit to prospective buyers on reasonable notice at reasonable times. If a lender forecloses, tenants have extra protection from quick removal.

title: Forms Connecticut Law Supplies
bodyText: Connecticut supplies these forms or required wording, which should be used as published: the notice to quit (substantially in the statutory form) and the statutory use-and-occupancy disclaimer; the Department of Housing's rental terms summary form (first page of every written lease from April 1, 2026), preoccupancy walk-through checklist and protected-tenant notice (for buildings of five or more units); the Judicial Branch right-to-counsel notice attached to notices to quit and eviction papers; and, for a lease with an option to buy, the Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities fair housing disclosure signed by the tenant-buyer and (for one to four units) the residential condition report. The Department of Housing also publishes optional standardized lease forms; no statutory lease form is mandatory. Statutory wording used as required does not violate the plain-language law.

title: Tenant Portals and Online Payments
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute on tenant portals as such, but several rules limit how you use one. You may not require online or electronic payment as the only way to pay rent or a security deposit; accept at least one paper method such as a check or money order. If your online payment system keeps a tenant from paying on time, the tenant gets five extra days that month before a late charge or a notice to quit for nonpayment. A processing fee may be left out of the advertised rent only if it reflects your actual cost and you offer a no-fee way to pay. A tenant who agreed to sign or receive documents electronically may later refuse further electronic transactions, and eviction, default and cure notices cannot be given through the portal alone.

title: Tenant Ledgers and Personal Information
bodyText: If a tenant or other occupant asks, you must give them a copy of the ledger (or equivalent accounting) for their unit showing charges, payments and any balance owed or overpaid; the statute sets no fee for it. Give a written receipt for every cash payment showing the date, amount and purpose. Keep applicants' and tenants' personal information, such as Social Security, driver's license and bank account numbers, safe from misuse and destroy it securely when you dispose of it. If you collect Social Security numbers in your business, you must publish or post a privacy protection policy. If computerized personal information is breached, you must notify affected Connecticut residents without unreasonable delay and within 60 days (unless an investigation reasonably shows harm is unlikely), notify the Attorney General no later than the residents, and, if Social Security or taxpayer ID numbers were exposed, offer at least two years of free identity theft prevention services.

title: Changing Rent or Other Terms
bodyText: You may raise rent only after giving the tenant written notice at least 45 days before the increase takes effect (for a lease of one month or less, notice equal to one full term), and not during a fixed lease term unless the lease itself provides for the increase (see the rent-escalation guidance). A tenant's silence is not agreement to the increase. Connecticut defines rent as all periodic payments due under the lease; treat a new or higher recurring fee the same way. A new building rule that substantially changes the lease is not valid unless the tenant agrees in writing; other changes need the tenant's agreement. For six months after a tenant's good-faith complaint, repair request or similar protected act you may not demand a rent increase, unless the tenant's household caused the problem through lack of due care or you became liable for a substantial increase in taxes or operating costs (not tied to fixing the complaint) at least four months before the demand, and then only by your prorated share of that increase.

title: No Sunsetting Tenant Laws
bodyText: As of October 9, 2026, none of Connecticut's core landlord-tenant statutes, including the good-cause protection for older and disabled tenants, the security deposit law and the notice-to-quit rules, is scheduled to expire. The 2026 session amended several of them (security-deposit enforcement, screening fees, unmetered utilities and a technical fix to the good-cause law) but repealed none. Check each year's new public acts.

title: Lease Translation
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to translate a lease, even if you negotiate it in another language. The Department of Housing publishes the rental terms summary form, the protected-tenant notice and its model lease forms in English and Spanish, and must add translations of the notice and the lease forms into the five most common languages by December 1, 2028; use the version your tenant reads best. From October 1, 2026, owners of residential buildings with elevators must post the state's English-and-Spanish elevator outage sign near each elevator's call buttons.

title: Service and Assistance Animals in Connecticut
bodyText: Connecticut fair housing law requires you to make reasonable accommodations in your rules for a tenant or household member with a physical, mental or learning disability, which includes allowing a needed service or assistance animal despite a no-pet rule and without pet fees. Connecticut has no separate statute on emotional support animals or the documentation you may request; the Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities posts guidance on the differences among service, emotional support and therapy animals and on how a landlord may tell them apart, so follow it. A person with a disability who visits your tenant may bring a service animal at no extra charge, though the animal's owner is liable for any damage it causes. Renting rooms in a home you live in, or a unit in a two-family house where you live in the other unit, is exempt.

title: Criminal Penalties for Refusing a Service Animal
bodyText: Refusing to let a person with a disability, or a person training a service animal, keep a service animal while visiting your tenant's home, charging them a fee other guests do not pay, or intentionally interfering with the animal's use is a crime in Connecticut (a class C misdemeanor). Separately, any violation of the state fair housing law, including refusing a reasonable accommodation for a tenant's assistance animal, is a class D misdemeanor; from October 1, 2026 that penalty is restated as the crime of hate crime by discriminatory housing practice. Owner-occupied rooms and owner-occupied two-family dwellings are exempt from both rules.

title: No Penalty for Misrepresenting an Animal
bodyText: Connecticut has no law making it a crime or civil violation to pass off a pet as a service or emotional support animal, in housing or anywhere else. Online registrations, certificates and vests prove nothing. When the need for an assistance animal is not obvious, evaluate the request as a reasonable accommodation, using the methods the Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities describes.

title: Tenant Electric Vehicle Chargers
bodyText:
You must approve a tenant's written request to install an electric vehicle charging station at the tenant's own dedicated parking space (an assigned space, garage, carport or exclusive-use spot) if the request meets the statute and your procedural approval process for modifications.

The duty applies to leases signed, extended or renewed on or after October 1, 2022 if you own 250 or more units, October 1, 2023 if you own 51 to 249, and October 1, 2024 if you own 50 or fewer.

It does not apply if chargers already serve at least 10 percent of designated spaces, parking is not part of the lease, there are fewer than five parking spaces, the property has low-income housing tax credits, or a housing authority manages it.

Before work starts the tenant must sign an agreement covering installation and removal, costs, electricity, any sharing with other tenants, liability insurance naming you, a removal bond or deposit withholding, and fixture status if the station is left behind.

You need not provide an extra parking space, and the installation must meet all codes, zoning and association rules.

title: Giving Notice of Parking Rules
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to hand over parking rules before the lease is signed or use a particular heading. A parking rule binds the tenant only if it is reasonable, applies fairly to all tenants, is clear, and the tenant had notice of it when signing the lease or when you adopted it; a new rule that substantially changes the lease needs the tenant's written agreement. If you tow from a lot at a building of five or more units, a condominium or a common interest community, you must also post conspicuous signs at the lot listing the parking rules whose violation can lead to a tow, and you must leave a 72-hour windshield notice before towing a car only because your parking permit has expired.

title: Towing From Your Property
bodyText:
A lease clause alone does not let you tow. In Connecticut you may have a vehicle towed from your property only if it is there without authorization, and you (or your agent) must sign the Department of Motor Vehicles written authorization form, under penalty of false statement, for each tow.

At a parking lot or garage at a building of five or more units, a condominium or a common interest community (lots at buildings of four or fewer units are exempt), you must first post conspicuous towing signs at every entrance (with the tow company's contact and fees) and a sign listing the parking rules that lead to towing, at least 48 hours before towing, except for cars blocking access, a fire hydrant, a traffic aisle or an accessible space.

You may not fine drivers or boot their cars.

Before towing a car only for expired registration you must leave a 14-day windshield notice, and for an expired parking permit at a residential lot a 72-hour notice.

You may not take any payment from the tow company, and if you tow improperly you must pay the owner's towing, storage and attorney's fees.

title: Parking Charges and Advertised Rent
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to offer parking separately from rent or regulate separate parking agreements. If a tenant must pay a recurring parking charge, or one that is billed monthly unless the tenant opts out, include it in the rent you advertise. A parking charge paid periodically under the lease likely counts as rent under Connecticut's definition (all periodic payments under the lease), so treat it like rent, including giving 45 days' written notice before an increase (one full term for a tenancy of one month or less).

title: Cannabis in Connecticut Rentals
bodyText: You may ban smoking or vaping cannabis anywhere on the property, but you may not ban a tenant from possessing cannabis or using it in other ways, such as edibles. You may not refuse to rent to someone, or treat them differently, because of a past conviction for possessing a small amount of cannabis, and you may not require tenants to take drug tests. These limits do not apply to a roomer renting part of a home, institutional or sober-living housing, or where following them would violate federal law or cost you a federal benefit, such as in federally assisted housing. Separately, unless federal law or federal funding requires otherwise, you may not refuse to rent to, or act against, a tenant solely because they are a qualifying medical-cannabis patient or caregiver (from October 1, 2026, including one qualifying from out of state); that rule has no roomer or sober-living exception. Connecticut lets adults and patients grow a few plants at their primary residence and gives landlords no express power to forbid it; a lease ban on home growing is unsettled.

title: No Disaster Guest Rule
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute letting a tenant house people displaced by a fire, storm or other disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, and none governing hotel guests displaced by a disaster. Your lease's guest terms apply, but consider consenting to temporary stays after a disaster, and apply any limit evenly so it does not fall more heavily on families with children or other protected groups.

title: Firearms and the Lease
bodyText: No Connecticut statute stops a residential lease from restricting firearms, and none protects firearms locked in a car in your parking area. This library offers no firearms clause. If you adopt a firearms rule, it must meet the general test for landlord rules, and you should get legal advice; federal and state criminal laws on carrying and storing firearms apply to tenants regardless of the lease.

title: Guests
bodyText: Connecticut does not regulate lease terms on guests or ban guest fees, apart from fair housing law and the general test for landlord rules. One specific rule: a guest with a disability (or a person training a service animal) may bring a service animal when visiting your tenant, and you may not charge them any fee you do not charge all guests. Your tenant is responsible for guests' conduct and damage, and a guest who moves in becomes an occupant under the lease's occupancy terms.

title: No Candidate Access Rule
bodyText: Connecticut has no law requiring you to let political candidates, campaign workers or voter-registration workers into an apartment building to reach tenants' doors. If your rental is a condominium or other common interest community unit, the association (not you) may not ban unit owners from displaying the state flag or signs about candidates or ballot questions, though it may regulate their time, place, size and manner.

title: No Window Unit Right
bodyText: Connecticut gives tenants no statutory right to install a window or portable air conditioner, and the lease need not say anything about it. A rule limiting window units must meet the general test for landlord rules (a safety or property-protection purpose, applied fairly and stated clearly). If you supply air conditioning, you must keep it in good working order, and the tenant must use it reasonably.

title: Plug-In Solar Devices
bodyText: Connecticut gives tenants no right to install a plug-in or balcony solar device over your objection, and lease restrictions on them are not regulated. From October 1, 2026, a small portable solar device (up to 1,200 watts, plugged into an ordinary outlet and not permanently attached) no longer needs the electric company's approval, but it must still meet building and fire codes and local rules, and that law does not override your lease or rules. Decide whether to allow such devices and say so in your rules.

title: Religious Items on the Entry Door
bodyText: If you rent out a condominium unit, you may not prohibit or interfere with your tenant attaching an object such as a mezuzah to the unit's entry door or door frame for religious reasons. The condominium's bylaws may still bar items that threaten health or safety, block the door, break the law or are obscene, and may limit items to 25 square inches on the frame and 4 square feet on the door. No Connecticut statute protects religious or cultural displays in other rentals, but a ban could raise fair housing concerns, and this library's lease rules leave room for displays the law protects.

title: When Your Rules Are Enforceable
bodyText: A building rule binds your tenant only if all of these are true: its purpose is the tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protecting your property from abuse, or fairly sharing services and facilities; it is reasonably related to that purpose; it applies fairly to all tenants; it is clear enough to tell the tenant what to do; and the tenant had notice of it when signing the lease or when you adopted it. A rule adopted after the lease is signed that substantially changes the lease is not valid unless the tenant agrees in writing. Valid rules become part of the rental agreement, and a material violation can lead to eviction after a written 15-day notice to cure where the breach can be cured.

title: Smoke From Other Units
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute on smoke drifting between units, and a lease clause making the tenant give up claims against you over drifting smoke is unenforceable to the extent it releases liability the law places on you. Smoking is already banned in passenger elevators, and you may ban smoking (including cannabis smoking and vaping) on the property in the lease. Whether the workplace smoking ban reaches enclosed hallways where your staff work is unsettled. Use the lease's smoking policy rather than a waiver.

title: Snow and Ice
bodyText: You must keep common areas, including shared walks, stairs and parking areas, clean and safe, and you cannot shift that duty to tenants. A written lease term may make a tenant clear snow and ice from areas only that tenant uses, such as the walk and driveway of a single-family home. If your town has adopted the state sidewalk law, the owner or the person in possession and control of land next to a public sidewalk is responsible for ice and snow on it and can be sued for injuries, so say in the lease who clears the public sidewalk and check your town's ordinance for clearing deadlines.

title: Flags and Signs
bodyText: No Connecticut statute protects a tenant's display of the U.S. flag, other flags or political signs against a landlord, so the lease's rules govern. If the rental is in a condominium or other common interest community, the association's rules must treat U.S. flag display consistently with federal law and may not ban owners' state flags or signs about candidates or ballot questions, only regulate their size, place and timing. This library's lease rules leave room for displays the law protects.

title: Tenant Cameras and Video Doorbells
bodyText: No Connecticut landlord-tenant statute addresses whether a tenant may install security cameras or video doorbells. The lease's alteration terms and your rules govern, and any rule must be reasonable and applied fairly. Consider allowing devices that do not damage the property, and be aware that cameras aimed at shared hallways or other units can raise privacy complaints between neighbors.

title: Waterbeds
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute on waterbeds or other water-filled furniture in rentals. You may forbid them or allow them on conditions, such as proof of insurance, through the lease or your rules; this library's lease bars them without your written consent.

title: Common Interest Community Notice: Timing
bodyText: If you are the developer (declarant) of a condominium or other common interest community, a successor declarant, or someone renting on the declarant's behalf, you must give the tenant written notice that the unit is in a common interest community before the rental agreement is entered into. The lease's own notice arrives only at signing, so also hand the tenant a separate written notice, and keep proof, before they sign. An individual unit owner renting out a unit has no duty to give this notice, though the association's rules still bind the tenant.

title: Certificates of Occupancy
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to tell a tenant about the unit's certificate of occupancy. But where your town requires one before a building is lived in, letting anyone occupy without it exposes you to a civil penalty of up to $20 a day per unit, for up to 200 days. Some towns also require a new certificate after every vacancy in buildings of three or more units (owner-occupied buildings of three or fewer units are exempt), and collecting rent for a unit rented without one carries the same penalty. Check your town's rules before each new tenancy.

title: No Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring you to disclose defective or corrosive drywall to a tenant. The crumbling-foundation (pyrrhotite) question appears on the state's residential condition report, which you must give only if you sell the property or lease it with an option to buy (one to four units). If a building condition affects health or safety, your duty to keep the unit fit and habitable and to meet housing codes applies regardless of disclosure.

title: Submetered Electricity
bodyText: Connecticut requires no lease disclosure about submetered electricity, but it tightly limits submetering. Only an entity approved by the Public Utilities Regulatory Authority may submeter electricity in a multifamily building, generally one powered by a Class I renewable source or combined heat and power, and it may charge no more than the utility's rate and nothing for common areas. For leases signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, a lease term making the tenant pay for utilities billed without a separate meter for the tenant's unit is unenforceable. Submetered utility costs may be left out of the rent you advertise.

title: No Flood Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to tell a tenant about flood zones or past flooding under an ordinary lease. If the lease gives the tenant an option to buy a one-to-four-unit property, you must give the state's residential condition report before signing, and it asks whether the property is in a flood hazard area. Insurers, not landlords, must tell renters' insurance customers that flood damage needs a separate flood policy. Telling tenants about known flooding is still good practice, and hiding a known defect can create liability under general law.

title: Foreclosure and Your Tenants
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to tell a prospective or current tenant that your property is in foreclosure. If a lender forecloses, a good-faith tenant keeps strong protection: the new owner takes the property subject to a bona fide lease until it ends (unless it sells to a buyer who will live there) and must give at least 90 days' written notice to vacate, eviction cannot start until the lease end date or 60 days after title passes (30 days for tenancies without a qualifying written lease), and any offer of money to leave must be at least the deposit with interest, two months' rent or $2,000, whichever is most. Voucher tenants have additional protection. The new owner also takes over the security deposits.

title: Renting Out a Condominium or CIC Unit
bodyText: If you rent out a unit in a condominium or other common interest community, the association's declaration, bylaws and rules bind your tenant. If your tenant violates them, the association may act against you and directly against the tenant: after notice and a chance to be heard it may fine you, the tenant or both, and if the violation is not fixed within 10 days after it notifies both of you, it may enforce your lease rights itself, including bringing an eviction. Association rules may restrict leasing only to meet mortgage lenders' requirements, and only if notice is recorded on the land records. If you fall behind on common charges, in the association's collection or lien-foreclosure case a court may appoint a receiver to collect the sums you owe while the case is pending.

title: No Code-Violation Disclosure Duty
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to tell a prospective tenant about open housing-code violations, inspection orders or condemnation orders. Your duties to comply with housing codes and keep the unit fit and habitable apply regardless, a tenant can complain to the code agency and later sue to have the rent paid into court, and some towns require a certificate of occupancy after each vacancy.

title: Connecticut's Lead Abatement Duties
bodyText:
Besides the federal lead disclosure for pre-1978 housing, Connecticut requires the owner of any dwelling with toxic levels of lead where a child under six lives to remediate it.

When such a child lives in the unit, defective lead-painted surfaces (including exterior and common-area surfaces) must be abated, intact lead surfaces need a written lead management plan within 60 days of the inspection results, and you may not avoid abatement by evicting the family.

If an inspection finds toxic lead, within two days you must post a warning notice on each entrance to the unit or affected common area, and give residents a summary of the inspection and the state's lead safety information.

A child's elevated blood lead level triggers a health department investigation and remediation orders, and evicting a tenant who complains to the code or health agency can be retaliation.

Connecticut has no lead-safe certificate you must obtain or attach to the lease, and no state lead notice due at signing or renewal.

title: No Meter Conservation Charge Notice
bodyText: Connecticut has no energy-efficiency charge attached to a meter that you must disclose to a new tenant. If you financed energy improvements through the state's on-bill repayment program, the repayments stay with the utility account of the customer who took the loan (and pass to later owners with notice); the utility cannot bill those repayments directly to a tenant who takes over service because you failed to pay.

title: No Meth Lab Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring you to disclose that methamphetamine was made or used in a rental, to report a suspected drug lab, or to test or clean up before renting. Contamination that makes a unit unfit is still covered by your duty to keep the unit fit and habitable and to meet health and housing codes, and concealing a known hazard can create liability under general law.

title: No Military Zone Disclosure
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to disclose that a rental is near a military installation or in an aircraft noise or accident potential zone, and gives tenants no termination right on that basis.

title: No Mold Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring you to disclose mold to a prospective tenant or to use a mold form. Mold that threatens health or safety is still your responsibility under your duty to keep the unit fit and habitable and to meet housing and health codes, and a tenant can complain to the local code or health agency. The Department of Public Health publishes mold abatement protocols and standards for identifying, assessing and remediating mold in housing; they are guidance, not regulations.

title: No Ordnance, Demolition or Shared-Meter Disclosure
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to disclose a nearby former military ordnance site, a pending demolition permit, or a utility meter that serves more than one unit. Separately, in a lease signed or renewed on or after October 1, 2026, a term making a tenant pay for utilities billed without a separate meter for the tenant's unit is unenforceable, and if you leave utilities in your name unpaid, the utility must offer tenants service in their own names.

title: Pest Control Notices
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to give tenants a pest control or pesticide notice before treatment or at signing. A licensed pesticide application business you hire must, before agreeing to treat, give you and the resident of the property the key label information for each pesticide, and, once the state adopts the implementing regulations, must notify abutting owners or tenants who have asked for notice before applying a pesticide within 100 yards of the property line. Entering a unit for pest treatment still requires reasonable notice, and bed bug inspection and treatment follow the bed bug statute.

title: No Pet Eviction Fact Sheet
bodyText: Connecticut has no state fact sheet on pets and eviction that you must give tenants, and its eviction statutes have no special rule for animals left behind. Plan with the tenant, the state marshal and local animal control if an eviction involves pets.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule
bodyText: Connecticut has no law like California's Proposition 65 requiring landlords to warn tenants about exposure to chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm. Specific hazards are governed by their own rules, such as the federal lead disclosure and Connecticut's lead abatement duties.

title: No Property-Tax Rent Statement
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to tell tenants how much of their rent goes to property taxes, annually or when rent changes. Tenants who apply for state renter's relief programs may ask you for rent information, which you are not required by statute to supply. A rent increase that passes through a substantial property-tax increase is one of the increases the anti-retaliation law allows, if limited to the prorated share of the increase.

title: No Radon Disclosure Requirement
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to test for radon or disclose radon results to a tenant under an ordinary lease. If the lease gives the tenant an option to buy a one-to-four-unit property, the residential condition report you must provide asks whether a radon test was done and asks you to attach the result. Testing is still a good idea in high-radon areas, especially for basement and ground-floor units.

title: Recycling
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring you to tell tenants where and how to recycle. State law requires everyone who generates household trash to separate the items the state designates for recycling, and each town enforces this by ordinance. You must provide proper trash receptacles and arrange for removal, and tenants must put their waste in them; tell tenants where recycling goes and follow your town's rules.

title: Rental Terms Summary Form
bodyText: For any written lease you give a tenant on or after April 1, 2026, including a renewal, the first page must be a completed copy of the Department of Housing's Standardized Rental Terms Summary Form, in English and Spanish. The form lists the property address, every tenant, the landlord and the person signing for the landlord, the point of contact for management and maintenance, the lease start and end dates, the total periodic rent, and every other charge the tenant must pay periodically, even one the tenant can opt out of (noting any opt-out). The total rent you show must include all required periodic fees, the same way your advertised rent must. If you provide a written lease without the form, you are liable to the tenant for a civil penalty equal to one month's rent, and the court may also award the tenant reasonable attorney's fees and costs. Download the current form from the Department of Housing website; this library's lease is built to sit behind it.

title: Connecticut Disclosure Checklist
bodyText: Before the tenant signs: disclose whether the unit or a contiguous unit you own has bed bugs (not for single-family unattached homes); if you are a condominium or other community's developer, give written notice that the unit is in a common interest community; if the property has a private well, give the state's well-testing information; for pre-1978 housing, give the federal lead disclosure and pamphlet; and for a lease with an option to buy a one-to-four-unit property, give the residential condition report. In the lease: the rental terms summary form as page one, the fire sprinkler notice in 12-point bold where the building must have sprinklers (with the last maintenance and inspection date if the system is operative), any recorded environmental activity and use limitation, and the names and addresses of your manager and agent for notices (by the start of the tenancy). At signing or renewal in buildings of five or more units: the state's protected-tenant notice. After signing but before move-in: offer a walk-through using the state checklist. Within 30 days of receiving a security deposit: tell the tenant the amount and the bank holding it. If you charged a screening fee: give the applicant the report (or how to get it) and the receipt.

title: No Code Variance Notice
bodyText: Connecticut has no state rule requiring you to give tenants a copy of, or attach to the lease, a variance from the health or housing code. A local health or code agency that grants a variance may impose its own conditions, so follow the variance's terms.

title: No Sex Offender Registry Notice
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to tell tenants about the state sex offender registry or about registered offenders living nearby, and no lease notice is prescribed. If you screen applicants using registry information, apply your criteria consistently and lawfully.

title: No Offender Residency Rule
bodyText: Connecticut has no state law limiting where registered sex offenders may live, no crime for leasing to two registered offenders who live together, and no occupancy duty for landlords near schools or child care. Any screening or occupancy policy you adopt is governed by fair housing and screening rules.

title: Lease Layout Rules
bodyText: Connecticut has no general rule on font size or first-page placement for lease disclosures, and no single-family occupancy notice.
