Three layout rules do apply: the state rental terms summary form must be the first page; the fire sprinkler notice, where required, must be in at least 12-point bold type of one font; and the whole lease must meet the plain-language law's standards, including readable type and bold or otherwise prominent section headings.

title: Lawful Source of Income Protection
bodyText: You may not refuse to rent to someone, set different terms, or advertise a preference because their income comes from a lawful source, which Connecticut defines as Social Security, SSI, housing assistance (including vouchers), child support, alimony or public or state-administered assistance. Statements like "no Section 8" are prohibited. You may deny an applicant whose total income, counting all lawful sources, is insufficient, but apply the same standard to everyone. The rule does not apply to renting rooms in a single-family home you live in or a unit in a two-family house where you live in the other unit. Violations can bring a discrimination complaint and are a crime.

title: Which Buildings Need the Sprinkler Notice
bodyText:
You must include the fire sprinkler notice in the lease if state law, the State Fire Safety Code, the State Fire Prevention Code or another regulation required your building to have a sprinkler system, whether or not one is actually working.

By statute this includes any building of more than four stories built for human occupancy, and residential buildings occupied mainly by people 65 or older that have more than four stories, or more than 12 units if built or substantially renovated on or after January 1, 1997; the State Fire Safety Code and State Building Code, which are based on national model codes, may require sprinklers in other buildings too, such as some newer apartment buildings.

If you are not sure, ask your local fire marshal or building official, or simply include the notice, stating truthfully whether the building has an operative system and, if so, the last maintenance and inspection date, printed in at least 12-point bold type.

title: Deaths, Crimes and Illness on the Property
bodyText: You do not have to tell a prospective tenant that a past occupant had a reportable disease, or that the property was suspected to be the site of a death or a felony, and you cannot be sued for not disclosing it. But if a prospective tenant who is making a good-faith offer tells you or your agent in writing that knowing whether the property was the site of a suspected homicide, other felony or suicide matters to their decision, you must answer in writing through your agent, consistent with privacy laws, or have your agent state in writing that you decline to answer. Physical defects are a different matter and are not covered by this rule.

title: Tenant Rights Statements
bodyText: Connecticut does not require private landlords to hand tenants a general statement of tenant rights. The required notices are the rental terms summary form on page one of the lease and, in buildings of five or more units, the state's protected-tenant notice. Housing authorities must also give each tenant, at the first lease signing and every year, contact information for management, the local health department and the Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities, plus the Judicial Branch's guide to landlord and tenant rights.

title: Condominium Conversion and Tenant Purchase Rights
bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide rent cap or general just-cause eviction law, so no lease notice about one is required. If you convert a rental building into a condominium or other common interest community, though, tenants have strong rights: at least nine months' written conversion notice before they must leave, an exclusive 90-day right to buy their own unit, a bar on offering it to anyone else on better terms for the next nine months, notice of who later contracts to buy it, the right to end their lease early on 30 days' notice, and, for lower-income tenants who move, a relocation payment.

title: Renting an Accessory Dwelling Unit
bodyText: Unless your town has opted out, Connecticut zoning must allow at least one accessory apartment (called an accessory dwelling unit from October 1, 2026) as of right on each lot with a single-family home, either attached or in a separate structure. The town may not require the occupants of the main home and the accessory unit to be related or employed by each other, impose a minimum age, require separate utility billing, require more than one parking space, or require periodic permit renewals, though it may prohibit using the unit for short-term or vacation rentals. Renting the unit long term is a normal residential tenancy, subject to all the usual landlord-tenant rules; check your town's zoning regulations and opt-out status before renting.

title: Casualty and Mitigation Rules Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: A Connecticut lease cannot take away the tenant's statutory rights if fire or another casualty substantially impairs the unit: no rent while the impairment lasts, the right to move out and end the lease by notice within 14 days, or a proportional rent reduction for a partly usable unit (unless the tenant caused the damage). Lease terms that conflict with these rules are unenforceable. The law also requires you to try to re-rent the unit at a fair rent when a tenant abandons it or breaches, which limits what you can collect. Whether a lease can waive that duty is not settled, so don't include a term that tries to. If you don't make reasonable efforts to re-rent an abandoned unit, the lease is treated as ended on the date you learned of the abandonment.

title: Families With Children
bodyText: You may not refuse to rent to, or set different terms for, families with children, and you may not advertise a preference against them. Your occupancy limit must be a reasonable one that applies to every occupant regardless of age and is consistent with state and local occupancy codes. Connecticut requires no lease clause about children. The familial-status rule does not apply to qualifying housing for older persons or to a building of four or fewer units where you live in one of the units.

title: No Confession of Judgment
bodyText: A Connecticut lease may not include a clause letting you enter a court judgment against the tenant without a hearing (a confession of judgment or warrant of attorney). Any such clause is unenforceable; you must sue and give the tenant the chance to defend, both for possession and for money.

title: Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act
bodyText: Connecticut's Unfair Trade Practices Act (CUTPA) covers renting and offering to rent residential property, so unfair or deceptive conduct in advertising, leasing or managing a rental can be a CUTPA violation. A tenant who loses money because of it can sue for actual damages, and the court may add punitive damages, attorney's fees and orders to stop the practice; the tenant need not show harm to the public. Some other laws that affect landlords are enforced through CUTPA, such as the rules for safeguarding tenants' Social Security numbers (enforced by the state, not by tenant lawsuits); the ban on rent-setting software is enforced separately under Connecticut's antitrust law. Whether CUTPA reaches a particular practice, or a landlord who rents only one or two units, depends on court decisions, so assume it applies to you. Using unenforceable lease terms, hiding fees or misstating tenants' rights are the kinds of practices most likely to draw a CUTPA claim.

title: Protecting a Victim's Information
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring you to keep confidential the sworn statement, police or court records, or protective order a tenant gives you to end the lease early or to get the locks changed after family violence or sexual assault. Treat them as confidential anyway: share them only with staff who need them, never with the person named in the order, and store them securely. The state's address confidentiality program substitute address binds government agencies, not landlords, but honor a tenant's request to use it for mail where you can. Fair housing law forbids refusing to rent because someone is a victim of domestic violence.

title: No Employee Background-Check Mandate
bodyText: Connecticut does not require you to run background checks on maintenance staff or property managers who have keys to tenants' units. Control keys carefully and give notice before entry as the law requires; careful hiring and key control also reduce your liability risk.

title: Making the Tenant Pay Eviction Costs
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute aimed at eviction penalty clauses, but it limits what you can shift to the tenant. A lease term making the tenant pay your attorney's fees is unenforceable to the extent it exceeds 15 percent of any money judgment against the tenant. If your lease makes the tenant pay your attorney's fees, a tenant who wins a suit or counterclaim based on the lease is entitled to fees too. You recover court costs with a judgment and may recover the marshal's removal expense from the tenant, but you may not charge a move-out fee, and a flat "eviction fee" or penalty risks being an unenforceable penalty or a disguised fee. Damages for the tenant's breach are the unpaid rent and other actual losses, reduced by your efforts to re-rent.

title: No Waivers of Your Legal Liability
bodyText: A Connecticut lease may not say that the tenant releases you from, or limits, any liability the law places on you, or that the tenant will indemnify you for that liability or its costs. Clauses like "Landlord is not liable for any injury or damage" or "Tenant will hold Landlord harmless from all claims" are unenforceable to the extent they reach your own legal responsibility, including your negligence and your repair and code duties. A lease may still make the tenant responsible for damage the tenant or the tenant's household or guests cause.

title: Connecticut Fair Housing Protected Classes
bodyText: In Connecticut you may not refuse to rent, set different terms, steer, misrepresent availability, or advertise a preference based on race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, gender identity or expression, sexual orientation, civil union or marital status, age, lawful source of income, familial status, physical, mental or learning disability, status as a veteran, or status as a victim of sexual assault or trafficking; you also may not refuse to rent to someone because they are a victim of domestic violence. Separately, you may not refuse to rent or set different terms because of an applicant's or household member's erased criminal record, unless you rent rooms in a unit you live in or live in a building of four or fewer units. You must also make reasonable accommodations and allow reasonable modifications for disability. Except for sexual orientation and civil union status, which have no owner-occupant exemption, state law exempts renting rooms in a single-family home you live in and a unit in a two-family house where you live in the other unit (and, for families with children only, owner-occupied buildings of up to four units); the federal Fair Housing Act's advertising ban still applies to those landlords. Violations can lead to a complaint with the Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities, and discrimination under the main fair housing statutes is also a crime.

title: No Foreign Ownership Restriction
bodyText: Connecticut does not restrict foreign nationals, foreign companies or so-called foreign adversaries from owning or leasing residential property. State law expressly lets any alien, whether or not living in the United States, hold, acquire, lease, inherit and transfer real estate as fully as a native-born citizen. Federal rules (for example, on sanctioned persons) may still apply.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute specifically about charging tenants for fines a town or the state imposes on you. But a lease cannot make a tenant indemnify you for liability the law places on you. Whether that bar covers a fine a town or the state imposes on you is not settled, so the safe course is not to pass on fines for your own code violations, such as failures in repairs, heat or common areas. If a tenant's own violation of the tenant duties (for example, improper trash disposal or damage) caused the fine, you may be able to recover it as damages. A condominium or homeowners association may impose reasonable fines on a tenant directly for rule violations after notice and a chance to be heard.

title: Immigration or Citizenship Questions
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant and fair housing statutes do not specifically forbid or require asking an applicant or tenant about immigration or citizenship status. Fair housing law does bar discrimination based on national origin and ancestry, so any such question must be applied the same way to everyone and must not be a pretext. From July 1, 2026, Connecticut's data privacy law also covers anyone who collects or uses 'sensitive data', which includes information revealing citizenship or immigration status: you may collect it only when reasonably necessary, only with the person's clear consent, and you must protect it. Unless a housing program you participate in requires immigration verification, the simplest course is not to ask.

title: Jury Trials and Jury Waivers
bodyText: In Connecticut there is no right to a jury in a summary process (eviction) case, so a lease clause waiving a jury does nothing for getting possession. In other civil cases, such as a suit for unpaid rent or damages over $250, either side may ask for a jury, and the state constitution protects that right. A Connecticut lease may not make the tenant give up rights under any state statute unless that statute expressly allows the waiver; the jury statute allows the parties to agree to a trial by the judge, but it is unsettled whether a waiver signed in a lease before any dispute counts. This library does not offer a jury waiver for Connecticut.

title: Using a Prohibited Lease Term
bodyText: Connecticut has no specific penalty for putting a prohibited term in a lease; the term is simply unenforceable. Other rules still make a sloppy lease costly. If your written lease does not start with the state's standardized rental terms summary form, or you otherwise break that statute's rules, the tenant can recover a civil penalty of one month's rent, and the court may also award attorney's fees. If your lease makes the tenant pay your attorney's fees, a tenant who wins is entitled to fees too. And trying to enforce terms the law forbids could be treated as an unfair or deceptive practice under the Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act, with damages and attorney's fees. No statute settles this, so assume it could.

title: Plain Language Lease Requirement
bodyText: Connecticut's plain language law covers every residential lease signed by a tenant renting for personal, family or household use, so your lease must be written in plain language. It qualifies in one of two ways. Either it substantially meets the general tests: short sentences and paragraphs, everyday words, 'you' and 'we' or the parties' names, simple active verbs, readable type, ink that contrasts with the paper, bold or prominent section captions, spacing between sections and from the page edges, and clear, coherent organization. Or it fully meets the objective tests: fewer than 22 words per sentence on average and none over 50; fewer than 75 words per paragraph on average and none over 150; fewer than 1.55 syllables per word; no type smaller than 8 points; at least 3/16 inch between paragraphs and 1/2 inch margins; printed section captions in bold of at least 10 points; and lines averaging no more than 65 characters. Wording a statute, regulation, agency or court requires or authorizes, and the legal description of the property, do not count against you. A lease that fails is still enforceable, but the tenant can recover $100 plus up to $100 in attorney's fees, unless you tried in good faith to meet the general tests. A tenant cannot waive these rights. No Connecticut law sets a separate minimum type size for the whole lease, though some notices have their own type rules, such as the fire sprinkler notice.

title: Other Lease Terms the Law Limits
bodyText: The list of banned lease terms is not the only limit on a Connecticut lease. A lease also may not: let you collect rent for a period when you are not meeting your basic repair and code duties; require rent or the security deposit to be paid only by electronic transfer; charge an application fee, move-in fee, move-out fee or any other up-front charge beyond a security deposit, the first month's rent, a key or special-equipment deposit and the capped tenant screening fee; require a security deposit above two months' rent (one month's rent for a tenant 62 or older); shift repairs to the tenant except under a written, good-faith agreement for specified tasks, which outside a single-family home cannot cover work needed to make the unit fit or code-compliant; or set terms that differ because of a protected characteristic. A liquidated damages clause may also need a signed boldface acknowledgment. No Connecticut statute specifically bars charging tenants a home-warranty deductible, but a charge for a repair that is your legal duty runs into the rule against waiving the tenant's statutory rights.

title: Questions About Protected Characteristics
bodyText: Connecticut has no separate law that forbids simply asking an applicant about a protected characteristic, but asking is risky. Fair housing law bars any notice or statement about a rental that shows a preference or limitation based on race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, gender identity or expression, marital status, age, lawful source of income, familial status, disability, veteran status or victim status, and an application question can be that kind of statement or evidence of discrimination. From July 1, 2026, Connecticut's data privacy law also covers anyone who collects 'sensitive data', such as race or ethnicity, religion, health or disability, sexual orientation, citizenship or immigration status, status as a crime victim, Social Security and driver's license numbers, and financial account or card numbers together with the code or password needed to access the account; you may collect it only when reasonably necessary and with the person's clear consent. Ask only what you need to apply your written criteria, such as income, rental history and references. You may ask for proof of age or disability when a law makes it relevant, for example to confirm a tenant's protection from eviction in a building converted to a condominium.

title: No State Owner-Occupancy Rental Limit
bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide law limiting rentals of homes in single-family zones to owners who live on the lot. State law instead governs how towns may regulate accessory apartments, though a town may opt out of that law. Check your town's zoning regulations, which may set their own rules for accessory apartments and rentals.

title: No Radiator Cover Requirement
bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide rule requiring you to install covers on steam radiators when a tenant asks, and no required radiator-cover lease rider or notice. You must still keep heating facilities in good and safe working order, and your town's housing code may say more. Covering very hot radiators is a sensible precaution in units with young children.

title: Voucher Program Inspections
bodyText: Connecticut has no law that lets you turn down a tenant using a housing voucher or other rental assistance because the program will inspect the unit. Refusing to rent because a tenant pays with housing assistance is source-of-income discrimination under state fair housing law (unless you rent a room in your own single-family home or a unit in a two-family home where you live in the other unit); you may deny an applicant only because the applicant's income is insufficient. Treating the program's inspection or paperwork as a reason to refuse is likely to be treated as refusing because of the assistance itself. Don't refuse a tenant for that reason.

title: Protecting Tenant and Applicant Data
bodyText: Connecticut has no landlord-specific law listing what tenant information you may not disclose, but general privacy laws apply to you. You must safeguard documents and files containing someone's personal information (such as Social Security, driver's license, account, passport or alien registration numbers) from misuse by others, and destroy or make them unreadable before you throw them away. If you collect Social Security numbers in your business, you must publish or publicly display a privacy protection policy that protects their confidentiality, prohibits unlawful disclosure and limits access. If computerized data containing a tenant's name with a Social Security, identification, account or similar number is breached, notify each affected Connecticut resident without unreasonable delay and within 60 days, notify the Attorney General, and where Social Security or taxpayer identification numbers were exposed, offer at least two years of free identity theft prevention services. From July 1, 2026, Connecticut's data privacy law also covers anyone who handles 'sensitive data', such as racial or ethnic origin, religion, health or disability, sexual orientation, citizenship or immigration status, status as a crime victim, Social Security, driver's license and passport numbers, and financial account or card numbers together with the code or password needed to access the account: collect it only when reasonably necessary and with the person's clear consent, keep collection to what you need, and protect it. Share tenant information only as needed to run the tenancy or as the law requires.

title: Screening Applicants in Connecticut
bodyText: Connecticut has no single tenant-screening law, but several rules limit how you screen. Fees: the only applicant charge allowed is a capped tenant screening report fee, and you must give the applicant the report (or how to get it) and the receipt. Criminal records: you may not refuse to rent, set different terms or advertise a limitation because of an erased criminal record, which includes records erased by law, youthful offender records and criminal cases continued for more than 13 months; this does not apply to renting rooms in a unit you live in or a unit in a building of four or fewer units where you live. A person with an erased record may truthfully say the arrest never happened. You also may not refuse to rent because of a past conviction for possessing a small amount of cannabis, and generally may not require a drug test. Connecticut sets no conditional-offer or look-back rule for other convictions, so apply written criteria the same way to everyone. Income: you may turn down an applicant whose income is insufficient, but not because the income comes from housing assistance, Social Security, child support, alimony or public assistance; no statute caps the income-to-rent ratio you may use. Fair housing and data privacy rules also limit what you may ask.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant laws have no section letting a court strike an unconscionable lease term, unlike some states. Courts may still refuse to enforce a grossly unfair term under general contract law; don't count on a one-sided term holding up. Many one-sided terms are already unenforceable because the lease-terms statute bans them. Separately, in a town with a fair rent commission, a tenant can ask the commission to limit a rent or rent increase that is so excessive as to be harsh and unconscionable.

title: Water Heater Temperature
bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide rule setting a maximum water heater temperature or requiring you to reset a unit's water heater before each new tenant moves in. You must supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, unless the hot water comes from equipment in the tenant's exclusive control or from the tenant's own utility connection, and willfully failing to furnish hot water the lease requires is a crime. Setting tank heaters at about 120 degrees Fahrenheit is a common scald-prevention practice; check your town's housing code and the Public Health Code for local standards.

title: No Window Guard Requirement
bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide requirement to install window guards or window stops where children live, and no required window-guard notice or lease rider. You must still comply with the building and housing codes that apply to your property, which your town may enforce. Window stops or guards on upper-floor windows are a sensible precaution in units with young children.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Many Connecticut landlord-tenant notices must be written, and a lease cannot replace them with verbal notice. Your notices that must be in writing include: a notice to quit (in the statutory form); a notice of a lease violation that starts the cure period; a rent increase notice at least 45 days ahead (one full term for a tenancy of one month or less); the names and addresses of your manager and agent for notices; notice that you have sold the property to a good-faith buyer, if you want to end your liability for later events; the result of a bed bug inspection within two days; the notice to elderly or disabled tenants in buildings of five or more units about their eviction protections; and, for a developer renting in a common interest community, notice that the unit is in one. A tenant's notice of your failure to make repairs, and a tenant's termination notice for an unremedied breach or as a victim of family violence or sexual assault, must also be written. A tenant may report bed bugs orally or in writing, and you may give reasonable written or oral notice before entering. When in doubt, put it in writing and keep a copy.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Connecticut Leases
bodyText:
No Connecticut statute deals specifically with arbitration clauses in residential leases.

The arbitration act makes a written agreement to arbitrate an existing or later dispute valid, enforceable and irrevocable except on grounds that would undo any contract, and before a dispute arises neither side may give up the right to a lawyer at the arbitration (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 52-407dd, 52-407ff).

The catch is the lease statute: a lease may not have the tenant waive rights under any state statute unless that statute allows it (§ 47a-4(a)(1)), and in most civil cases either side may claim a jury (§ 52-215). Eviction cases have no jury, and possession stays in court anyway.

Federal law also matters here: the Federal Arbitration Act overrides state rules that block arbitration directly or indirectly (for example, a rule against giving up a jury).

On that basis the library offers an optional clause, "Binding Arbitration of Money Claims" clause: money claims only, with possession, small claims, security-deposit, injury, emergency and government-agency matters kept out, every remedy and the right to a lawyer kept, the arbitration fees above a court filing fee paid by you, a 30-day opt-out for the tenant, and separate initials.

A court here could still refuse to enforce it; if one did, the dispute would simply go to court.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Connecticut follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42a-3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42a-1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (Conn. Gen. Stat. chs. 830 and 832 searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Connecticut's courts do is case law, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: Which Documents Qualify a Victim for Each Protection
bodyText: Connecticut's two tenancy protections for victims use different documents and different time rules, so check each request against the statute it relies on. To end a lease early, a victim of family violence or sexual assault must give you at least 30 days' written notice that includes a sworn statement and either a police or court record of the violence dated not more than 90 days before the notice, or a signed statement from an employee of the Judicial Department's Office of Victim Services or the Office of the Victim Advocate dated not more than 30 days before the notice (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11e(a)-(b)). Those time limits run back from the date of the tenant's notice, not from the move-out date (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11e(b)(2)). A lock change works differently: the tenant must give you a copy of a protective or restraining order issued by a Connecticut court, or a registered foreign order of protection, that is in effect when the tenant asks and orders the other person to stay away from the tenant's home or a minimum distance from the tenant (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7b(a)). There is no age limit on that order, but a police report or victim-services letter alone does not trigger the lock-change duty (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7b(a)). Connecticut has no separate eviction defense with its own document list. If you doubt that a termination notice meets the statute, your remedy is to ask the housing session for an injunction, not to ignore the notice (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11e(f)). Keep copies of what the tenant gives you confidential and use them only to apply these rules.

title: EV Chargers When the Tenancy Ends
bodyText: When you must approve a tenant's electric vehicle charging station, the written agreement the tenant signs before work starts must deal with the end of the tenancy (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13b(e)). It must cover removal of the station and its infrastructure, and payment of the costs of damage, removal and replacement (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13b(e)(1), (4)). It must require the tenant either to post a surety bond equal to the cost of removing the station or to let you withhold all or part of the security deposit at the end of the tenancy for damages caused by the tenant's failure to meet your removal requirements (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13b(e)(7)). It must also require the tenant to agree that the station becomes a fixture of the property if the tenant does not remove it when the lease ends (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13b(e)(8)). Any deposit deduction still follows the itemized-statement and deadline rules of the deposit statute (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21). Practical step: in the agreement, say whether you want the station removed or left in place, and inspect the parking space and electrical work at move-out.

title: Shared EV Chargers and Common Parking
bodyText: Connecticut's tenant charging-station law reaches only a tenant's dedicated parking space: a space in the tenant's separate interest, or a common-area spot the tenant has exclusive use of, such as an assigned space, garage or carport (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13b(a)(1)). It does not require you to let a tenant install a charger in unassigned common parking, and you need not provide an additional parking space to accommodate a charger (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13b(c)). If another tenant will use a charger a tenant installs, the requesting tenant must sign a cooperative agreement with you and the other tenant on electricity metering and each party's duties, and the participating tenants pay its costs, including attorney's fees and metering costs (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13b(e)(5)). The duty does not apply at all if you already provide chargers for tenants at 10 percent or more of the designated parking spaces, if parking is not part of the lease, or if the property has fewer than five parking spaces (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13b(f)(1)-(3)). Any charger, shared or not, must meet state and federal law, local ordinances, zoning and any covenants (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13b(d)). Practical step: if you install shared chargers yourself, put the access rules and any charging fee in written rules or the lease, and meter the charger so common-area electricity is not billed to tenants who do not use it.

title: No Professional Carpet Cleaning Rule
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute letting you require professional carpet cleaning at move-out, and no condition-and-age test for carpet or paint deductions. What the law does say: you may keep part of the security deposit only for damages you suffered because the tenant failed to meet the tenant's obligations, which are unpaid rent or utility payments owed to you, the tenant's statutory duties, and an unpaid lock-change cost (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(a)(14), (d)(1)). Those duties include keeping the part of the premises the tenant uses as clean and safe as its condition permits, and not wilfully or negligently damaging or defacing the premises (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11(b), (f)). Any deduction must be listed, by nature and amount, in a written statement delivered within 21 days after the tenancy ends or 15 days after you receive the tenant's forwarding address, whichever is later, or you owe twice the deposit (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(d)(2)). A lease cannot make the tenant waive rights under these statutes (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(1)), and money collected in advance, other than first month's rent or a key or special-equipment deposit, is a security deposit, so a prepaid cleaning fee counts toward the deposit limit (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(a)(11)). The cautious course: do not charge a fixed professional-cleaning fee whatever the carpets' condition; deduct only the actual, reasonable cost of cleaning or repairing carpet the tenant left dirtier or damaged in breach of those duties, and keep move-in and move-out photos and receipts.

title: No Designated-Repairer Rule
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute that lets you name, in the lease, who must do repair work the tenant arranges at your expense. The tenant's only self-help remedy of that kind covers essential services: if you are required to supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service and fail to for reasons within your control, the tenant may give you notice and buy reasonable amounts of the service and deduct the actual and reasonable cost from rent (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13(a)(1)). That right does not arise until the tenant has given you reasonable written or oral notice, or if the tenant, the tenant's family or a guest caused the problem (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13(c)). Connecticut tenants have no general repair-and-deduct remedy for other repairs. A lease cannot waive or narrow the essential-services remedy (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(1)), so do not make use of your contractor a condition of it. Repairs a tenant agrees to do for you are a different thing: they need a written, good-faith agreement listing the specified tasks, and in a building other than a single-family home they cannot include work needed to bring the unit up to code or make it fit and habitable (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(c), (d)). Practical step: give tenants an emergency repair number and the name and address of the person managing the property, which you must disclose anyway (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-6(a)), and answer service failures fast.

title: No Required Fitness Statement in the Lease
bodyText: Connecticut does not require your lease to state that you will deliver or keep the unit fit for habitation. The duty applies anyway: you must comply with the tenement and lodging house law and the building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises fit and habitable (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(a)(1)-(2)). A lease cannot let you receive rent for any period in which you are not meeting that duty (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4a). A lease also cannot make the tenant waive these rights or release you from liability the law places on you, and such a term is unenforceable (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(1), (3), (b)). So a sentence promising a habitable unit is harmless, while an 'as is' sentence or a disclaimer of your repair duty does not work. What a Connecticut lease must carry is different: since April 1, 2026, a completed Department of Housing rental terms summary form as the first page of any written rental agreement (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7d(d)), and, where the building must have sprinklers, the sprinkler notice in at least 12-point bold type (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-3f(b)).

title: No No-Notice Entry for Scheduled Services
bodyText: Connecticut has no rule letting a lease authorize entry without notice for regularly scheduled services such as pest control, filter changes or smoke alarm checks. Supplying necessary or agreed services is one of the reasons a tenant may not unreasonably refuse you entry (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-16(a)). But you must give reasonable written or oral notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times, except in an emergency (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-16(c)). Without the tenant's consent you may enter only in an emergency, during a tenant's extended absence as the statute allows, under a court order, or after the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-16(d)). A lease term giving up the notice right is unenforceable, because a lease may not make the tenant waive rights under the landlord-tenant chapter (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(1), (b)). If you run a recurring service, give the tenant a written schedule and a reasonable reminder before each visit, and a new notice if a date changes; no statute says a schedule printed in the lease is enough on its own. Entering unlawfully, or making repeated demands for entry that harass the tenant, exposes you to the tenant's court remedies (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-18a).

title: No Showing-Notice Waiver
bodyText: Connecticut has no procedure letting a tenant waive or shorten the entry notice for showings, in the lease or in a separate signed document. You may show the unit to prospective or actual buyers, lenders and tenants, and the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-16(a)). Connecticut sets no fixed number of hours: you must give reasonable written or oral notice and come at reasonable times, except in an emergency (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-16(c)). During a tenant's extended absence you may also enter at reasonable times to show the unit, unless you and the tenant agreed otherwise (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-16a). A lease cannot make the tenant waive rights under the landlord-tenant chapter, and such a term is unenforceable (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(1), (b)), so a standing waiver of showing notice should not be relied on. A tenant can still agree to a particular showing on short notice; record that consent for each showing. Repeated showing demands that unreasonably harass the tenant let the tenant recover at least one month's rent plus attorney's fees, or end the lease (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-18a). If a tenant unreasonably refuses a showing, your remedy is a court order or termination, with damages and attorney's fees (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-18).

title: No Separate Nonrefundable-Deposit Notice
bodyText: Connecticut has no rule requiring a separate written notice, when you collect a deposit, that part of it is nonrefundable. That is because Connecticut has no nonrefundable deposit: any advance rental payment, other than first month's rent or a deposit for a key or special equipment, is a security deposit (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(a)(11)). A security deposit remains the tenant's property, subject only to your security interest for the tenant's obligations (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(c)). It must go into an escrow account (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(h)(1)), it counts toward the limit of two months' rent, or one month's rent for a tenant 62 or older (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(b)), and it must be returned with interest less itemized damages within the statutory deadline (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21(d)). Don't give a tenant a notice or receipt calling any part of a deposit nonrefundable. The notice that matters for fees is different: an advertised rent must include every fee the tenant must pay on a periodic basis, with limited exceptions such as a pet fee or deposit (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7d(a)-(b)).

title: No Small-Landlord Remedy Exemption
bodyText: Connecticut has no notice or other procedure that lets a landlord with only a few units opt out of tenants' repair remedies, including the right to pay rent into court. Any tenant who claims you have not met your repair or code duties may, at least 21 days after complaining to the municipal code agency, sue in the housing session and pay each month's rent to the court clerk (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14h(a)-(b), (h)). While the clerk holds rent equal to what is due, you may not evict for nonpayment (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14h(h)). The statute has no exception for owner-occupied buildings or small landlords. The landlord-tenant chapter's exclusions turn on the kind of occupancy, not the number of units: institutional residence, a buyer under a contract of sale, fraternal or social organization housing, transient hotel or motel stays, a condominium owner, and a live-in personal care assistant (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-2(a)). A lease cannot waive these remedies (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(1)). Do not add a small-landlord exemption notice to a Connecticut lease. If a tenant pays into court, you may move at any time to end the payments once the violations are corrected (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14h(i)).

title: Which Repair Problems Trigger Tenant Remedies
bodyText: Connecticut's repair duties and tenant remedies are tied to how serious a problem is. Your code duty covers building and housing codes 'materially affecting health and safety' (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(a)(1)), alongside the broader duty to keep the premises fit and habitable and facilities and appliances you supply in good and safe working order (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(a)(2), (4)). A tenant with a lease longer than one month may end it on 15 days' written notice only for a material noncompliance with the lease, or a noncompliance with your statutory duties that materially affects health and safety, that you do not fix in time (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-12(a), (c)). The essential-services remedies apply only to failures to supply heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service that are not caused by conditions beyond your control (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13(a)). Rent stops after a fire or other casualty only if enjoyment of the unit is substantially impaired (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14(a)). None of these remedies is available for a condition the tenant, the tenant's family or guests caused (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 47a-12(b), 47a-13(c)). A minor or cosmetic problem does not end the lease, but it is still your duty to fix what the codes and the fit-and-habitable standard require. A good-faith repair request also starts the six-month retaliation protection, whatever its size (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-20(3)).

title: Shifting Repair and Maintenance Duties to the Tenant
bodyText:
Connecticut lets you shift some repair and maintenance work to the tenant, but only by written agreement and within limits that depend on the building.
- In a single-family residence, you and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant handles waste receptacles and removal and supplies water, hot water and heat, and also does specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, if the deal is made in good faith and not to evade your obligations (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(c)).
- In any other dwelling unit, you may agree only that the tenant does specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling, and only if the agreement is in good faith and in writing, the work is not needed to cure a code violation or to make the unit fit and habitable, and the agreement does not reduce your duties to other tenants (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(d)).

The statute does not require any particular consideration, such as a rent reduction, or a separate document; a written lease term listing the tasks can satisfy it. List each task specifically: a general promise that the tenant will 'make all repairs' is not an agreement to perform specified work.

Your duty to comply with codes and keep the premises fit and habitable stays with you except where the tenant intentionally made the unit unfit (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(a)(2)). A term making the tenant waive the statute's protections is unenforceable (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(1), (b)).

title: Tenant Repair Remedies and Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: Connecticut tenants have four statutory remedies when repairs are not made. First, a tenant with a lease longer than one month may give written notice of a material breach and the lease ends if you do not fix it within 15 days (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-12(a), (c)). Second, if you fail to supply heat, water, hot water, electricity, gas or another essential service for reasons within your control, the tenant may buy the service and deduct its cost, or get substitute housing with rent abated if you do not restore it within 48 hours, or, if the failure is wilful, end the lease and recover two months' rent or double damages, whichever is greater (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13(a)-(b)). Third, rent stops while fire or other casualty substantially impairs the unit (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14(a)). Fourth, at least 21 days after complaining to the municipal code agency, a tenant may sue in the housing session and must pay the last agreed rent to the court clerk each month; while the clerk holds the rent due, you cannot evict for nonpayment (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14h(b), (h)). The court can order repairs, appoint a receiver, award damages including a retroactive rent abatement, and use the money held for repairs (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14h(e), (g)). How you get the money: you may move at any time to end the payments into court, and if the court finds the violations corrected it enters judgment on how the money held is distributed (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14h(i)). If the tenant stops paying the clerk, you may move to dismiss the case (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14h(h)). You may also counterclaim for an order that the tenant meet the tenant's own duties (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14h(f)). None of these remedies covers conditions the tenant's household or guests caused (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 47a-12(b), 47a-13(c)).

title: Seasonal and Vacation Rentals
bodyText: Connecticut has no special lease form or no-court removal procedure for seasonal rentals. Three rules matter. First, transient occupancy in a hotel, motel or similar lodging is outside the landlord-tenant chapter (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-2(a)(4)). A stay of less than 30 days is transient unless the unit is the occupant's primary residence from the start, and a stay of 30 days or more is not transient unless the unit is not the occupant's primary residence and the stay is for less than 90 days (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-2(c)). Second, a seasonal rental that is not transient is an ordinary tenancy: when its fixed term ends, a tenant who stays over must still be removed by a notice to quit for lapse of time and a summary process case, not by changing the locks (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23(a)(1)(A)). Third, once you win, the post-judgment stays that can delay a move-out by up to six months do not apply to housing in a resort community customarily rented or occupied on a seasonal basis (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 47a-36(3), 47a-39). The five-day automatic stay after judgment still applies (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-35(a)). The security deposit statute has no seasonal exception, so a deposit on a seasonal lease follows the usual limits, escrow and return rules (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-21). Practical step: put a definite start and end date in a seasonal lease; without a definite term, a tenancy is month to month (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-3b).

title: No Exemption Notice Needed
bodyText: Connecticut has no statewide rent cap or general just-cause eviction law with an exemption that a lease must announce, so no lease statement telling tenants a property is exempt is required. The rule closest to one runs the other way. Tenants who are 62 or older, or who have a qualifying long-term disability (or live with a family member who is or does), in a building or complex of five or more units or a mobile manufactured home park may be evicted only for the reasons the statute lists, and their rent increases must be fair and equitable (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23c(a)-(c)). For those buildings, you must give every tenant the Department of Housing's notice of these protections when you rent the unit and at every renewal, whether or not the tenant qualifies (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23c(e)(1)). The rule applies by building size, so a building with four or fewer units simply falls outside it; no notice of that is needed. In a common interest community, the rule covers conversion tenants and qualifying tenants whose landlord owns five or more units there (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23c(a)(2)). Separately, local fair rent commissions hear tenants' complaints about excessive rent, increases and fees, except for seasonal rentals of 120 days or less a year (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 7-148b(a)-(b)). They also need no exemption notice.

title: Housing for Your Employees
bodyText: Connecticut has no disclosure form for housing you provide to an employee, but it has its own eviction rules. When a farm employee, domestic servant, caretaker, manager or other employee lives in housing the employer furnishes and the job ends, whether the employee quits, is let go or stops reporting for work, and the employee does not leave, you must give at least three days' notice to quit on the statutory form and may then bring a summary process case (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 47a-30(a)-(b), 47a-23(a)(5)). The court may grant only a stay of execution that is reasonable and fair, and never more than 15 days; the longer hardship stays do not apply (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-30(c)). The same longer stays are also unavailable for farm housing occupied by a tenant who works a substantial part of the time on that farm, and for dwelling space given to domestic servants, caretakers, managers or other employees as part or all of their pay for work connected with the premises (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-36(1)-(2)). A personal care assistant who lives in a disabled employer's own home as a benefit or condition of the job is outside the landlord-tenant chapter entirely (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-2(a)(6)). You still need a court judgment to remove a former employee; do not change the locks. Practical step: put the housing terms, including that the right to occupy ends with the job and any rent charged, in writing at hiring.

title: No Separate Fast Track for Criminal Activity
bodyText: Connecticut has no separate expedited eviction track for drug or violent crime; every eviction is a summary process case, which is already a fast procedure in which pleadings must advance at least one step every three days (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-26c). What criminal conduct changes is narrower. For a serious nuisance, which includes inflicting or credibly threatening bodily harm on another tenant or you, substantial wilful destruction, conduct that presents an immediate and serious danger, and using or allowing the premises to be used for prostitution or the illegal sale of drugs, you may skip the 15-day notice to cure and serve a notice to quit directly (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-15). If a tenant is convicted of keeping a house of prostitution there, or of a gambling violation there, the lease is void and you may sue for possession without a notice to quit (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-31). After a judgment for nuisance or for illegal or immoral use, the tenant cannot apply for the longer hardship stay of execution (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-37(a)), though the five-day automatic stay still runs (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-35(a)). And an execution may be enforced against a person found to have sold drugs at the premises without waiting for execution against other occupants (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-26h(c)). You still need a court judgment and a state marshal; arrests alone do not end the tenancy.

title: No Statutory Right to Pay and Stop the Eviction
bodyText: Connecticut gives a tenant no statutory right to stop a nonpayment eviction by paying the arrears before judgment, and no right to reinstate a lease that ended for nonpayment. A tenant who has not paid within the grace period, nine days after rent is due (four days for a week-to-week tenancy, with five more days if your online payment system blocked payment), may be served a notice to quit (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-15a(a); Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23(a)(1)(D)). Two rules work like redemption. First, if you accept rent knowing it is overdue, you waive your right to end the tenancy for that missed payment (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-19); after the notice to quit, accept money only for use and occupancy with the statutory disclaimer (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23(e)). Second, after a nonpayment judgment, the tenant may apply for a stay of execution only by depositing the full arrearage with the court clerk within five days (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-37(a)), and the stay can then last up to three months, on terms that may require paying use and occupancy (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-39). Nothing stops you from agreeing to a payment plan and withdrawing the case; put any such deal in writing, usually as a stipulated judgment the court can enforce.

title: Type Size and Layout for Connecticut Leases
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute that sets one minimum type size for a whole lease and bars a landlord from using small print as evidence. Type size comes in through the plain language law, which covers every written lease of a residential dwelling made for personal, family or household purposes (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-151(b)). A lease passes if it substantially meets general tests, which include type of readable size, ink that contrasts with the paper, captions in boldface or that otherwise stand out, and spacing that separates paragraphs and sections from each other and from the page borders (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-152(b)(5)-(8)). Or it passes if it fully meets objective tests, which include no type smaller than eight points, at least three-sixteenths of an inch between paragraphs, half-inch margins and printed section captions in boldface of at least ten points (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-152(c)(7)-(10)). A lease that fails is still enforceable, but the tenant can recover $100 in statutory damages plus up to $100 in attorney's fees, unless you tried in good faith to meet the general tests (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 42-154, 42-155(b), 42-157(a)). One required lease notice has its own size rule: where the building must have a sprinkler system, the sprinkler notice must be printed in at least 12-point boldface type of uniform font (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-3f(b)-(c)). Practical step: print the whole lease in at least 10-point type with bold captions, and the sprinkler notice in 12-point bold.

title: Plain Language Required; No Consumer-Restrictions Statement
bodyText: Connecticut's plain language law reaches residential leases, but it has no statement of consumer restrictions, no list-of-waivers requirement and no Attorney General preapproval procedure. The law applies to any written agreement under which an individual leases a residential dwelling primarily for personal, family or household purposes, with no dollar limit for leases (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-151(b)). The lease must pass either the general plain-language tests or the objective readability tests (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-152(a)-(c)). Wording a statute, regulation, agency or court decision expressly requires or authorizes does not count against you (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-156(a)). A lease that fails stays enforceable, but the tenant can recover $100 plus up to $100 in attorney's fees (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 42-154, 42-157(a)). No damages are awarded for failing the general tests if you tried in good faith to meet them, and no class action may be brought (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-155(b)-(c)). A tenant may not waive these rights (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-157(c)). Separately, a Connecticut lease cannot make the tenant waive rights under the landlord-tenant statutes at all, so there is no list of waivers to disclose (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(1)). Since April 1, 2026, the first page of a written lease must be the Department of Housing's rental terms summary form (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7d(d)).

title: Leases of Indian Reservation Land
bodyText: Connecticut has no communal-land approval rule for ordinary residential leases, but it limits leases of state-recognized Indian reservation land. The chapter covers the Paucatuck Eastern Pequot reservation in North Stonington, the Golden Hill Paugussett reservations in Trumbull and Colchester, the Schaghticoke reservation in Kent and the Mashantucket Pequot reservation in Ledyard (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47-63). Reservation land the state held in trust on October 1, 1989 stays in trust to prevent alienation, and, except as the statutes expressly provide, any conveyance by an Indian of land belonging to a tribe's estate is void (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47-60(a)). Each tribe decides who may live on its reservation land and may lease that land for no more than 25 years (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47-64(a)-(b)). A lease of reservation land to a tribal housing authority for housing needs the approval of the Commissioner of Energy and Environmental Protection (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47-66d). The state recognizes the tribes as self-governing, with power to decide residency on reservation land and to make contracts (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47-59a(b)). Land held in trust by the United States for a federally recognized tribe is governed by federal law. If you are offered a lease of, or a sublease on, reservation or tribal land, confirm with the tribe, and for federal trust land with the federal Bureau of Indian Affairs, who may grant it and what approval it needs before you sign or collect rent.

title: Recording a Connecticut Lease
bodyText: Connecticut never requires you to record an ordinary residential lease, and recording does not change any right between you and your tenant. Recording matters only for a lease for life or for a term of more than one year, or a lease with a renewal right or an option to purchase. Such a lease is not effective against anyone other than the landlord, the tenant and their heirs and successors, such as a later buyer or lender, unless it is in writing and executed, witnessed, acknowledged and recorded like a deed (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47-19). Instead of the whole lease, you may record a notice of lease. It must be executed and recorded the same way and list the parties and their addresses, the lease's date, the term with its start and end dates, a description of the property, any renewal or extension right, any purchase option's exercise deadline, and where the lease is on file (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47-19). Practical step: for a one-year residential lease, recording is unnecessary. For a longer lease or one with a purchase option, the tenant may want a notice of lease recorded on the town land records to protect the term against a sale or foreclosure; a notice keeps the rent and other terms off the public record.

title: When a Lease Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Connecticut's statute of frauds bars a lawsuit on an agreement for an interest in real property, or one not to be performed within one year, unless the agreement or a memorandum of it is in writing and signed by the person it is enforced against or that person's agent (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-550(a)(4)-(5)). That rule does not apply to an oral lease for one year or less once the tenant, or someone claiming under the tenant, has actually occupied the premises during any part of the term (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-550(b)). So an oral lease of up to one year is enforceable after move-in, while a longer lease must be in a signed writing. Connecticut has no five-year or other long-lease exclusion from tenant protections: the landlord-tenant statutes apply whatever the length of the term. A separate recording rule applies to a lease for life or for more than one year, or one with a renewal or purchase option: it binds a later buyer or lender only if the lease or a notice of lease is executed, witnessed, acknowledged and recorded like a deed (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47-19). That is a priority rule; it does not make an unrecorded lease invalid between you and the tenant. Since April 1, 2026, any written lease you provide must start with the Department of Housing's rental terms summary form (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7d(d)).

title: Who May Represent an LLC or Corporation Landlord in Court
bodyText: If your rentals are owned by an LLC, corporation or other entity, plan on hiring a Connecticut lawyer for an eviction case. A person not admitted as an attorney may not practice law or appear as an attorney for another in any court of record, and a violation is a class D felony (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 51-88(a)(1), (b)(1)). The statute lets a person plead only in that person's own cause (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 51-88(d)(2)). The court rules define the practice of law to include representing any person in a court, and define a 'person' to include a corporation, company, partnership and any other entity (Conn. Practice Book § 2-44A(a)). Whether an owner or member may appear for a single-member LLC as its 'own cause' is case law; the cautious course is to have a lawyer file and appear. Two narrower rules help. A notice to quit may be given by the owner or lessor or by the owner's legal representative, attorney-at-law or attorney-in-fact, so a manager you appoint can sign it (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23(a)). And in small claims cases, such as a claim for unpaid rent or damages after move-out, a corporation may be represented by an officer, manager or local manager, though no one other than a lawyer may take a fee for representing a party (Conn. Practice Book § 24-6(a), (c)). Small claims is not the court for an eviction.

title: Hunting and Trapping on Rented Land
bodyText: Connecticut does not say whether a tenant of rented land gets hunting or fishing rights; the lease decides. Three statutes bear on it. No person may hunt on private land without the permission of the owner of the land (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 26-65(b)). That text names only the owner, so a tenant's permission alone may not be enough for a guest to hunt; the cautious course is for you, as owner, to give or refuse permission in writing. Trapping is different: no one may set or attend a trap on another's land without carrying the written permission of the owner or lessee, or the owner's or lessee's agent (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 26-72). Entering or staying on premises to hunt, trap or fish without a license or privilege to do so is criminal trespass in the third degree, punished as a class B misdemeanor with a fine of $500 to $1,000 (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-109(a)(2), (b)). A Connecticut resident landowner, and that landowner's spouse and children, may hunt, trap or fish without a license on land the landowner owns or on leased land where the landowner actually lives, if the land is not used for club, fishing or hunting purposes (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 26-27(b)). Practical step: if you rent a farm or house with acreage, say in the lease whether the tenant may hunt, trap or fish, whether the tenant may invite others to, and that hunting by anyone needs your written permission.

title: Banning a Non-Tenant from the Property
bodyText: Connecticut's criminal trespass law lets you keep a non-tenant, such as a former tenant, a troublemaker or someone the courts have ordered away, out of parking lots, hallways and other common areas. A person commits criminal trespass in the first degree, a class A misdemeanor, by entering or staying in a building or other premises, knowing the person is not licensed or privileged to, after the owner or another authorized person personally told the person to leave or not to enter (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-107(a)(1), (b)). Entering or staying in violation of a restraining or protective order is also first-degree trespass (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-107(a)(2)). For the trespass law, each apartment or rented room not occupied by the person is a separate building (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-100(a)(1)). It is a defense that the premises were open to the public and the person followed all lawful conditions of access, or that the person reasonably believed the owner or someone empowered to license access would have let them in (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-110(2)-(3)). So give the person the order to leave or not to enter in person, put it in writing too, keep a copy, and tell police. A person a tenant invites into the tenant's own unit is the tenant's guest; deal with an unwanted guest there through the lease and the tenant, not by a trespass order, and never use trespass to remove a tenant or occupant, which needs a court eviction (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23(a)).

title: Pets Left Behind or Left Without Care
bodyText:
Connecticut's abandoned-unit procedure says nothing about animals: it covers inventorying, storing for 30 days and then disposing of 'possessions and personal effects' (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11b(d)). Do not treat a pet as property to be stored or thrown out.

The rule that matters is the animal cruelty law: anyone who has charge or custody of an animal and fails to give it proper food, drink or protection from the weather, or abandons it, commits a crime (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53-247(a)). So once you take a tenant's left-behind animal into your care, you take on that care duty.

Connecticut has no rule making someone who feeds an animal for a set number of days its owner. For dogs, a 'keeper' is anyone other than the owner who harbors or has possession of the dog (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 22-327(6)), and a town's feral-cat ordinance may treat anyone who harbors or regularly feeds a feral cat as its keeper (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 22-339d(a)).

The safer course is to call the local animal control officer, who may take into custody any dog or other domestic animal found neglected or abandoned and must notify the owner or keeper if known (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 22-332(a)). If an animal is in distress inside an occupied unit, you may enter without the tenant's consent only in an emergency (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-16(b)).

Practical step: ask tenants in writing to name someone who can care for or remove their animals if they are hospitalized, detained or move out, and keep that contact on file. The library's optional clause "Animal Care if Tenant Is Absent" records that contact and your permission to let them in.

title: When Rental Buildings Need Sprinklers
bodyText: Connecticut's sprinkler statute applies mainly to new construction and to a few building types. Any building to be built with more than four stories for human occupancy must have an automatic fire extinguishing system approved by the State Fire Marshal on each floor (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 29-315(a)(1)). Two retrofit deadlines have passed: hotels and motels of more than four stories by October 1, 1992, and residential buildings of more than four stories occupied primarily by elderly persons by January 1, 1995 (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 29-315(c), (d)(1)). 'Occupied primarily by elderly persons' means at least 80 percent of the available units have a resident aged 65 or older (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 29-315(d)(1)). A residential building of more than 12 units occupied or designed to be occupied primarily by elderly persons that got a building permit for new occupancy, or was substantially renovated, on or after January 1, 1997 also needs sprinklers on each floor (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 29-315(d)(2)). The State Fire Marshal may require sprinklers in other occupancies with special hazards (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 29-315(e)). Failing to install a required system carries a civil penalty of up to $1,000 a day (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 29-315(g)). The State Building Code and the Fire Safety Code are based on national model codes and can require sprinklers in other buildings, and the Fire Safety Code does not reach private dwellings occupied by one or two families except for its smoke and carbon monoxide alarm rules (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 29-252(a)(1), 29-292(a)(1)). If your building must have sprinklers, the lease must say whether it has an operative system, in 12-point bold type (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-3f(b)). Ask the local fire marshal what your building requires.

title: Code Editions Change Over Time
bodyText: Connecticut's building and fire codes are not frozen to a fixed edition; they are updated on a rolling basis. The State Building Code must be based on a nationally recognized model building code and revised to take in later revisions of that model code within 18 months after they are first published (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 29-252(a)(1)). It also includes any code, rule or regulation it incorporates by reference (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 29-252(a)(1)). The Fire Safety Code must be based on nationally recognized model fire and life safety codes and revised within 18 months after the model codes' revisions are first published, unless the State Fire Marshal and the Codes and Standards Committee certify a revision is not needed (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 29-292(a)(1)). One statute names a specific edition: the State Building Code had to incorporate the 2012 International Energy Conservation Code (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 29-256a(a)). Your landlord duties track whatever codes apply: you must comply with all applicable building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and a stricter local ordinance or building or fire code controls over the landlord-tenant statute (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7(a)(1), (b)). Because editions change, ask your local building official and fire marshal which editions apply to your building and any work you plan.

title: Time Limit to Sue for Rent or Damages
bodyText: Connecticut's landlord-tenant statutes set no special deadline for suing a former tenant, so the general limitation periods apply. A suit on a written lease, or on an implied contract or an account, must be brought within six years after the right of action accrues (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-576(a)). A suit on an oral lease, or one not signed by the tenant or the tenant's agent, must be brought within three years (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-581(a)). A claim for damage to the property framed as negligence must be brought within two years after the injury is first sustained or discovered, or reasonably should have been, and never more than three years after the act (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-584), and other tort claims within three years of the act (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-577). The period runs from when the right of action accrues (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-576(a)); for rent, the cautious course is to measure it from each installment's due date. Whether a partial payment or a written acknowledgment of the debt restarts the period is case law; do not count on it, and sue within the period measured from the earliest unpaid amount. Practical step: keep the signed lease and a rent ledger; a written, signed lease is what gets you the six-year period instead of three.

title: Who Can Be Served With Eviction Papers
bodyText: Connecticut does not provide for a lease naming someone to accept eviction papers for the tenant. The statutes fix service instead. A state marshal or other proper officer serves an attested copy of the notice to quit on each lessee or occupant, or leaves it at the person's place of residence (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23(c)). The summons and complaint follow the ordinary civil rule: left with the defendant or at the defendant's usual place of abode in Connecticut (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 52-57(a)). If a tenant is not a Connecticut resident, papers may be served on the person in charge of the premises, or otherwise as the statutes allow, at least ten days before the date to quit; if the tenant has gone to parts unknown, by newspaper notice (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23b). One rule names a third party by law: for a participant in the Secretary of the State's address confidentiality program, the Secretary of the State is the participant's agent for any summons, writ, notice or process (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 54-240l(a)). A state marshal must check the program list and, if the tenant is on it, serve two attested copies at the Secretary of the State's office or by registered or certified mail marked 'Address Confidentiality Program'. Service is effective when the Secretary receives the papers, and the Secretary forwards them within two business days (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 54-240l(b)-(d)). A lease clause appointing an agent would be a tenant waiver of these service rules, which a lease cannot impose (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(1)). Use the lease's notice clause for ordinary notices, and leave eviction service to the marshal.

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate for Rentals
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring a lead-safe certificate, periodic lead inspection or lead registration for rental housing, and none that must be attached to a lease. Connecticut's lead law is triggered by findings, not by renting. The owner of any dwelling where paint, plaster or other material is found to contain toxic levels of lead and where children under six live must remediate it through testing, abatement or management under the Department of Public Health's regulations (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-111c(a)). A local director of health who receives a report of a child's elevated blood lead level must investigate and order the person responsible for the condition to act (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-111(b)-(c)). Paint on interior surfaces of a rented one- or two-family dwelling, and of a tenement house, must not be cracked, chipped, blistered, flaking, loose or peeling so as to be a health hazard (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 47a-52(d), 47a-54f(b)). Anyone who detects a toxic level of lead must report it to the Commissioner of Public Health, who informs the owner and occupants (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-111b(3)). The Department's lead regulations add duties that start with an inspection report, not with renting: within two days of a report finding toxic lead that requires abatement, you must post a notice of at least 8 1/2 by 11 inches on each affected entrance and leave it up until the unit complies, give residents a summary of the inspection and post-abatement reports and the Department's lead information, and keep residents out of rooms where abatement is under way (Regs. Conn. State Agencies §§ 19a-111-3(e), 19a-111-7(a)). Where a child lives in the unit, defective lead surfaces must be abated, and you may not avoid abatement by evicting a family with a child (Regs. Conn. State Agencies § 19a-111-2(a)). For pre-1978 housing the federal lead disclosure still applies. The cautious course is to keep painted surfaces intact and use lead-safe work practices on any repair that disturbs old paint.

title: No State Lead Notice With the Lease
bodyText: Beyond the federal lead disclosure and pamphlet for pre-1978 housing, Connecticut's statutes require no state lead notice, certificate or information packet to be given with a lease or at renewal. The state's lead information flows a different way. The Department of Public Health must run an education program aimed in particular at owners of buildings built before 1978 (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-111b(1)). Local health directors give the state's lead information to the parents of a child with an elevated blood lead level, not landlords to tenants (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-111(a)). When anyone detects a toxic level of lead, the Commissioner of Public Health informs the owner and the occupants of the building (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-111b(3)). Owners must remediate toxic lead where children under six live, following the Department of Public Health's regulations (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-111c(a)). Those regulations set the testing, abatement and management steps, and their notice duties start with an inspection report, not with a lease: within two days of a report finding toxic lead that requires abatement, you must post a notice on each affected entrance, and you must give residents a summary of the inspection and post-abatement reports and the Department's information on lead and how to avoid exposure (Regs. Conn. State Agencies § 19a-111-3(e)). Keep the signed federal disclosure with the lease.

title: Tenant Remedies When You Breach the Lease
bodyText: If you materially fail to keep the lease, or fail to meet your statutory repair duties in a way that materially affects health and safety, a tenant with a lease of more than one month may give you written notice of the breach, and the lease ends if you do not fix it within 15 days (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-12(a), (c)). If the same breach recurs within six months, the tenant may end the lease on at least 14 days' written notice (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-12(a)). That remedy does not limit the tenant's other remedies (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-12(d)). The others include the essential-services remedies, including two months' rent or double damages for a wilful failure to supply heat, water, electricity or gas (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13(a)); no rent while fire or casualty substantially impairs the unit (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14(a)); and a court action with rent paid into court (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14h).
