A lease cannot let you collect rent for any period in which you are not meeting your repair and code duties (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4a). An unlawful entry, or harassing demands for entry, costs at least one month's rent plus attorney's fees (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-18a). Locking a tenant out, removing belongings or otherwise taking possession by force can lead to a court complaint and double damages (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 47a-43(a), 47a-46). Retaliating within six months after a good-faith complaint or repair request is also barred (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-20). Connecticut's lead law has no rule directing tenants to withhold rent until lead is abated; it works through health department orders to the owner (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-111(c)).

title: When Rent Stops or Is Suspended
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute that flatly bars you from demanding rent after a code officer's notice goes unanswered, but several rules stop or suspend rent. A lease cannot let you receive rent for any period in which you are not meeting your duties to comply with the codes and keep the premises fit and habitable (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4a). A tenant owes no rent while fire or other casualty substantially impairs enjoyment of the unit, unless the tenant caused the damage (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14(a)). If you fail to supply an essential service and the tenant moves to substitute housing, rent abates for the period of your noncompliance (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-13(b)). A local fair rent commission that finds, after a hearing, that a unit fails to comply with a health and safety ordinance, statute or regulation may suspend rent until you make the needed repairs, with the rent paid to the commission in escrow (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 7-148d(a)). And when a tenant pays rent into court in a repair action, that payment counts as payment to you, and you may not evict for nonpayment while the clerk holds the rent due (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14h(h)). The cautious course: once a unit has a serious code violation or casualty damage, do not demand full rent or serve a nonpayment notice until the condition is fixed or you have taken advice.

title: Late Fee Limits, Including Mobile Home Parks
bodyText: Connecticut caps late charges for ordinary tenancies and sets a separate cap for mobile manufactured home parks. For an ordinary dwelling, a late charge needs a valid written lease term and may be charged only after the grace period, nine days after rent is due (four days for a one-week tenancy), plus five more days when your online payment system kept the tenant from paying (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-15a(a)-(b)). The charge may not exceed the lesser of $5 a day up to $50, or 5 percent of the late payment, or 5 percent of the tenant's share where a government or charity pays part of the rent. Only one late charge may be assessed per late payment (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-15a(b)). A lease term charging earlier or more is unenforceable (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(8)-(9), (b)). In a mobile manufactured home park, the rental agreement may not allow a late penalty without at least nine days' grace, and may not allow a late penalty of more than 5 percent of the total rent for a space or lot, or 4 percent of the total rent for a home and lot together (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 21-83(a)(3)-(4)). Such a provision is unenforceable (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 21-83(b)). Connecticut's self-storage statute sets no late-fee figure, so it offers no comparison. Practical step: state the late charge in the lease as a dollar amount within the cap, and never stack a second charge on the same late payment.

title: Tenant Damage to Your Property Can Be a Crime
bodyText: Connecticut's penal code has offenses aimed at tenants who damage a landlord's property, separate from ordinary criminal mischief. A tenant who, with no reasonable ground to believe the tenant has a right to, intentionally damages the landlord's tangible property at the premises by more than $1,500 commits criminal damage of a landlord's property in the first degree, a class D felony (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-117e(a), (d)). Intentional damage over $250, or reckless damage over $1,500, is the second degree, a class A misdemeanor (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-117f(a), (d)). Reckless damage over $250 is the third degree, a class B misdemeanor (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-117g(a), (d)). These offenses use the landlord-tenant definitions of tenant, landlord and premises, and do not stop prosecution under any other statute (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-117e(b)-(c)). The landlord-tenant law separately requires every tenant not to wilfully or negligently destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises or let anyone else do so, and not to disturb neighbors or create a nuisance (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11(f)-(g)). Substantial and wilful destruction is a 'serious nuisance' that lets you go straight to a notice to quit (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-15). A criminal case is for the police and prosecutor; to recover the cost, use the deposit itemization or a civil claim, and keep photos, repair invoices and the move-in record.

title: Conviction for Prostitution or Gaming Voids the Lease
bodyText: Connecticut has a statute that makes the lease itself void after certain convictions. When a tenant is convicted of keeping a house of ill-fame in the unit, resorted to for prostitution or lewdness, or of violating a gaming law in the unit, the lease or rental agreement is void as of the conviction (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-31). You still recover possession through the ordinary summary process (eviction) procedure, but no notice to quit is required (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-31). The rule needs a conviction; an arrest or a suspicion is not enough. Without a conviction, a violation of the lease is a ground for a notice to quit (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23(a)(1)(C)). Using the unit for an illegal purpose also lifts the six-month bar on eviction after a tenant's complaint (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-20a(1)). And a serious nuisance, such as using the premises for prostitution or the illegal sale of drugs, lets you skip the 15-day cure notice (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-15). Owners should know the other side too: a person who owns or leases a building used for prostitution maintains a nuisance (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 19a-345), and a person in control of premises known to be used for prostitution who makes no reasonable effort to stop it commits a class A misdemeanor (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 53a-89). Keep the court record of the conviction with the eviction papers.

title: Collecting Rent Stays Tied to the Repair Duty
bodyText: Connecticut did not adopt the uniform act's rule that the right to receive rent cannot be separated from the landlord's maintenance duties by lease, assignment, deed or security instrument. It reaches a similar result in other ways. A rental agreement cannot let you receive rent for any period in which you are not meeting your duties to comply with the codes and keep the premises fit and habitable (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4a). 'Landlord' includes the owner, lessor or sublessor (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-1(4)). 'Owner' includes a mortgagee in possession (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-1(5)). If you do not give the tenant the written names and addresses of your manager and your agent for notices, the person you authorized to sign the lease is treated as your agent for your repair duties, with authority to spend rent collected from the premises on them (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-6(a)-(b)). If you sell to a good-faith buyer, you are relieved of liability only for events after written notice of the sale to the tenant (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-10(a)). Whether an assignment of rents to a lender or other party, standing alone, frees the assignee from the repair duties is not addressed by statute and rests on case law. The cautious course is to assume that whoever collects the rent must see that the repair duties are met.

title: No Required Emergency Number or Hotline in the Lease
bodyText: Connecticut does not require a lease to list an emergency repair number, a management website or a social-services hotline. What the statutes do require is narrower. You must tell the tenant in writing, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises and of the person authorized to receive notices, demands and service of process, and keep that information current (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-6(a)). The library's "Landlord Identification" clause does this. Separately, a tenant may name an emergency contact. If the sole occupant dies, you notify that contact and the next of kin before using the Probate Court procedure for the belongings, and the notice must give a telephone number and mailing address where you can be reached (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11d(a)). The library's optional "Death of a Sole Occupant" clause collects that contact. Giving tenants a number for urgent repairs is good practice, but it is your choice how to do so.

title: No Statute on Releasing Tenants' Energy Data
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute that lets a lease authorize a utility to release a tenant's energy usage data to the owner for benchmarking, and no building benchmarking requirement for private residential owners. The energy-data statutes that exist work at a different level. Electric distribution and gas companies must make energy consumption data for typical nonresidential buildings public, free of charge (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-245ii). They must also give a town's legislative body aggregate usage information by customer class that keeps individual customers confidential (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-245jj). State agencies may benchmark energy and water use in state buildings (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16a-37t). If you want a tenant's usage history, for example to set a utility allowance, ask the tenant to request it from the utility or sign the utility's own release form; do not put a blanket data release in the lease.

title: No Statutory Landlord Termination After an Environmental Event
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute giving a landlord a right to end a lease after an environmental public health event or a government order that makes occupancy unlawful. Its casualty statute gives rights only to the tenant. If fire or other casualty substantially impairs the unit and the tenant did not cause it, the tenant owes no rent while the impairment lasts. The tenant may move out and end the lease by written notice within 14 days, or, if continued occupancy is lawful, move out of the unusable part and pay reduced use and occupancy (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14(a)). If the lease ends, you return the security and prepaid rent, accounted as of the date of the casualty (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14(b)). A health department may order an unfit rented dwelling vacated within 24 hours to 10 days (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-52(e)). A lease may set its own termination terms, since a lease can end 'by reason of any expressed stipulation therein' (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23(a)(1)(B)). The library's optional "Fire or Casualty" clause gives you that right after a casualty, on 30 days' notice, without cutting the tenant's statutory rights. A landlord who still needs possession must use summary process, not self-help.

title: Charging Tenants for EV Charging: Utility, Scales and Tax Rules
bodyText: Owning an electric vehicle charging station does not by itself make you a utility, public utility or public service company (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-1(c)). Connecticut's weights-and-measures registration reaches public charging stations: each public electric vehicle charging station must be registered every year with the Commissioner of Consumer Protection, for a $50 fee (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 43-3(b)(1)). A public station is one at a publicly available parking space. That definition excludes a space that is part of a private residence and a space reserved for tenants, residents of a common interest development or residents of an adjacent building (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 16-19f(a)(6)-(7)). So a charger at a tenant's own or tenants-only space is not a public station, but one you open to the public is. On tax, the sales tax exemption covers electricity delivered through lines for use in a residential dwelling (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 12-412(3)(A)). No statute says whether a landlord's separate charge for charging, billed by use, is a taxable sale of electricity or of a service. Ask the Department of Revenue Services before billing by the kilowatt-hour. The cautious course is to fold charging into the rent or a flat parking fee, or have the tenant pay the utility directly on a separate meter. The tenant-installed charger rules are in "Tenant Electric Vehicle Chargers".

title: No State Rights Guide for Private Landlords
bodyText: Connecticut does not require a private landlord to give tenants a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights and responsibilities, before signing or at renewal, or to get a signed receipt for one. The required state forms are narrower. From April 1, 2026, a written lease must have the Department of Housing's completed standardized rental terms summary form as its first page (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7d(c)-(d)). In a building or complex of five or more units, or a mobile manufactured home park, you must give written notice of the protected-tenant rules whenever you rent, sign or renew (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23c(e)(1)). On fair housing, the Commission on Human Rights and Opportunities has the power to require anyone covered by the housing discrimination statutes to post notices of those statutes (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 46a-54(14)). Its regulations do not use that power for housing: their only posting rules are for employers. Displaying the Commission's fair housing poster in any rental office is still good practice. See "Tenant Rights Statements" and "Rental Terms Summary Form".

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure in Leases
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring a lease of shoreline property to include a disclosure about the public's right of access to the shore, or any coastal, beach, tidal or flood-zone disclosure in a residential lease. Connecticut's coastal laws regulate structures, dredging and development along the coast rather than the content of leases. If you rent waterfront property, do not describe the boundary between your land and the public shore in the lease unless you know where it lies.

title: No Special District Disclosure in Leases
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring a lease to disclose or acknowledge that the property lies in a special services district, tax district or other special taxing district, or to pass on such a district's charges in a set form. Towns may create special services districts with their own charges, and those charges fall on property owners. If you want the tenant to bear any such charge, it must be part of the rent stated in the lease. Connecticut requires recurring charges to be included in the advertised rent (see "Advertised Rent Must Include Recurring Fees").

title: Student Housing and the Landlord-Tenant Act
bodyText: Connecticut has no student-housing statute imposing duties on private landlords who rent to students. Its rule is an exemption, and a narrow one. The landlord-tenant act does not govern residence at an institution, public or private, if it is incidental to providing educational or similar services (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-2(a)(1)). That exemption does not apply to an arrangement created to avoid the act (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-2(a)). The statute speaks of residence at an institution, so it plainly reaches a school's own dormitories. A private building rented to students, including one a school master-leases, is not obviously residence 'at an institution', and whether it qualifies rests on case law. The cautious course: a private landlord renting to students should treat the lease as fully covered by the act, with its deposit, notice, repair and eviction rules. Separately, a municipal tax provision describes rental housing for students and dormitories of 20 or more beds (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 12-66c), but it imposes no lease duty.

title: Key Control and Biometric Door Systems
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute requiring a key-control policy or background checks for employees with key access in large apartment complexes. Your lock duties come from the general repair and safety duties and the domestic violence lock-change rule (see "Lock Changes for Tenants With Protective Orders"). A fingerprint, face or other biometric door-entry system is different. From July 1, 2026, the Connecticut Data Privacy Act applies to any person doing business in Connecticut that controls or processes consumers' sensitive data, whatever its size (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-516(2), as amended by P.A. 25-113, § 6). Sensitive data includes biometric data (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-515(40), as amended by P.A. 26-64, § 12, eff. Oct. 1, 2026). Biometric data means automatic measurements of biological characteristics, such as a fingerprint or iris, used to identify a specific person (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-515(4)). A tenant is a consumer: a Connecticut resident not acting in a commercial or employment role (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-515(8)). Since October 1, 2026, a controller may process sensitive data only when reasonably necessary for the purposes it is processed for, and with the consumer's consent (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-520(a)(1)(D), as amended by P.A. 26-64, § 14). The Act says it does not restrict processing to prevent or respond to security incidents or illegal activity (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-524). Whether that covers a building's door system is not settled, and case law. The cautious course: get each tenant's separate written consent before enrolling them, offer a key or fob instead, and delete the data when the tenancy ends. The library does not offer a biometric-consent clause; if you use a fingerprint or face entry system, you can add your own clause.

title: Tenants' Unions Are Protected From Retaliation
bodyText: Connecticut protects tenants who organize through its retaliation statute rather than a stand-alone right to organize. For six months after a tenant has organized or become a member of a tenants' union, you may not sue to recover possession, demand a rent increase or cut the tenant's services (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-20(5)). The same six-month bar follows good-faith repair requests, code complaints, fair rent commission complaints and rent-into-court actions (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-20(1)-(4)). Connecticut's statutes do not give private-housing tenants a right to meet in common areas, distribute literature door to door or bring in outside organizers, as some states do. They also do not require you to recognize or bargain with a tenants' union. Tenant organizations have formal roles only in public housing: a housing authority must recognize an elected jurisdiction-wide tenant organization and work with it on resident participation plans before major redevelopment (Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 8-41(b), 8-64c(b)). A lease term barring tenants from joining or forming a union cannot be used to evict them within the protected period, and the cautious course is to leave any such term out.

title: No Utility Disclosure Attachment; Shared-Meter Billing Barred
bodyText: Connecticut does not require a utility-billing disclosure attached to the lease. It also does not require you to give a prospective tenant past heating or cooling bills or energy-use data on request. Instead, from October 1, 2026, Connecticut bars most of the billing such a disclosure would describe. For rental agreements entered into or renewed on or after that date, a lease cannot require the tenant to pay for utilities billed to the tenant if no separate meter measures utilities delivered only to the tenant's unit (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(11), added by P.A. 26-113, § 1). Such a term is unenforceable (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(b)). A lease also cannot require a heat or utilities surcharge when heat or utilities are included in the rent (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4(a)(10)). In listings, the advertised rent may leave out utilities only if they are submetered under the state's submetering statute or paid directly to a utility company and vary month to month (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7d(b)(3)). So in a shared-meter building, include those utilities in the rent; do not allocate them among tenants by formula.

title: Partial Unfitness in Subsidized Tenancies
bodyText: Connecticut has no statute saying how rent is reduced when part of a subsidized unit becomes unfit, or whether the reduction is figured on the total rent or only the tenant's share. The general rules apply. If fire or other casualty not caused by the tenant substantially impairs the unit and continued occupancy is lawful, the tenant may move out of the unusable part. The tenant's liability for use and occupancy is then reduced in proportion to the drop in the unit's fair rental value (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14(a)(2)). The rent is accounted as of the date of the casualty (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-14(b)). A lease cannot let you receive rent for a period in which you are not meeting your code and fitness duties (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-4a). For a voucher tenancy, the housing agency's own rules on abating its payment for failed inspections also apply. When a subsidized unit is partly unusable, the cautious course is to reduce the tenant's portion in proportion, tell the housing agency in writing at once, and not collect from the tenant any amount the agency withholds.

title: No Truth in Renting Statement
bodyText: Connecticut has no truth-in-renting statement: there is no state-published statement of landlord and tenant rights that private landlords must give tenants or post. The required state documents are the Department of Housing's standardized rental terms summary form, which must be the first page of a written lease from April 1, 2026 (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-7d(c)-(d)), and, in buildings or complexes of five or more units and mobile manufactured home parks, written notice of the protected-tenant rules at each rental, signing or renewal (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-23c(e)(1)).

title: Leasing From a Life Tenant
bodyText: Connecticut has no usufruct, but its nearest equivalent, a life estate, has a statutory eviction rule. If a tenant rents from a person who owns the property only for life, then when that life tenant dies, the person entitled to the reversion or remainder may bring summary process (eviction) against the tenant (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-29). An eviction the life tenant started may be continued in the remainderman's name after the life tenant's death (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-29). The statute does not say whether the lease ends automatically at the life tenant's death or what notice the tenant gets. That rests on case law. The cautious course for a landlord who holds only a life estate: tell the tenant in the lease that you hold a life estate and the lease may end at your death, and do not sign a term longer than you can secure from the remainderman. A remainderman who wants possession should still serve a notice to quit and use summary process. The library does not offer a life-tenant notice clause; if you hold the property only for life, you can add your own clause.
